According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created. By shrinking down the LED backlighting that powered older TVs since flat screens first gained traction in the late 2000s, TV makers have found a way to deliver brighter TVs with richer, more accurate colors without relying on expensive new display technologies.

The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot latest multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.

Just as importantly, they often offer great bang for the buck, especially when you're looking for a larger screen size—let’s say 75 inches or higher. As malleable as they are cost-effective, mini-LED is the secret sauce behind some of the best TVs on the market, even outdoing premium OLED screens in metrics like brightness and color expansion.

We’ve tested the top mini-LED TVs around, from entry-level options to groundbreaking flagships, to help you find the best options for your money.

I picked the top mini-LED TVs after sampling the best the market has to offer from brands like LG, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Hisense. I tested four of the TVs directly, while two of them were tested by Popular Mechanics staff and recommended based on that testing.

It has been revealed that my evaluation was based on performance traits like brightness, color vibrancy and accuracy, image processing and upscaling, black levels, and overall contrast. For my testing process, I used objective measurements like brightness and color accuracy with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software, as well as subjective testing using a wide library of familiar content, from test demos to films and TV shows via 4K HDR Blu-rays and streaming. I also weighed usability features like smarts and gaming options, overall design, and size options for those interested in the ever-expanding big-screen TV market.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been reviewing TVs and audio technology for well over a decade at publications like Wired, Business Insider, Digital Trends, and others. I’ve reviewed virtually every kind of TV and display technology available, from budget screens to premium RGB LEDs. I’ve gone hands-on with the best fresh mini-LED TVs from brands like Samsung, LG, Sony, TCL, Hisense, Roku, and others, along with competing tech like OLED and QD-OLED, each of which has its advantages. Few things give me more pleasure than finding people the best tech for their money at every performance level and budget.

RGB LED, which uses tri-colored red, green, and blue light clusters for enhanced color expression, was the hot fresh display tech at the start of 2026. Virtually every major brand debuted some form of RGB Mini-LED, kick-starting a premium Mini-LED alternative to OLED.

Recent findings suggest that when TCL introduced its own RGB TV for 2026, the RM9L, it seemed less excited about the RGB factor, and more interested in hyping up its exclusive new mini-LED tech, Super Quantum Dots (SQD). The QM8L makes it easy to see why.

SQD is an advanced version of regular quantum dots: tiny nanocrystals that emit pure, bright colors when exposed to light to enhance colors and brightness. Fancy tech aside, the results speak for themselves. The QM8L offers incredible brightness, far outshining its predecessor, the QM8K, alongside expansive colors that are as accurate as they are vibrant.

The newly introduced display offers other benefits, including fantastic black levels with very little light bleed, and reduced off-angle performance loss for most settings. Image processing has also improved, getting closer to the clarity and upscaling in top flagships from brands like LG and Samsung. The result is a premium picture that comes tantalizingly close to OLED displays in terms of contrast between the lightest and darkest images, and details that seem to pull you into the screen.

The TV’s Google TV interface is another plus, offering easy setup and extras like the ability to add albums from your Google Photos library as screen savers. Modern connectivity provides top-tier gaming features across inputs, and the sound isn’t bad either, thanks to built-in Bang & Olufsen speakers. Given that you can grab a 65-inch QM8L for as low as $1,000 or less on sale, it’s an easy pick for the best mini-LED TV available.

In many ways, entry-level TVs like the Hisense U6SF Pro are the best way to gauge how far TV tech has come in recent years. You just don’t expect a TV this cheap to look this good, from punchy brightness and naturalistic colors to minimal light bleed that lets you watch even challenging scenes in a dark room without being pulled out of the moment.

Industry observers note that one sacrifice at this price is the TV’s black levels, which don’t look as rich as pricier mini-LED TVs, let alone self-lit OLED displays. Because of that, even though the TV’s brightness rises above anything you can stream, it can look less striking than step-up models. On the other hand, its matte-like screen does a great job of diminishing ambient light and even direct light reflections for a good picture day or night. That’s something I didn’t expect to see at this level.

It has been revealed that you’ll get some handy features, including support for all major HDR formats and dual HDMI 2.1 ports with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) up to 144 Hz for PC gaming, another impressive get at this price. I find the TV’s Fire TV smart system a little clunky, but it includes some cool extras, like Ambient Mode that displays free artwork. TCL’s QM6K is a good alternative thanks to its friendlier Google TV smart system, but it can’t match the U6SF Pro’s performance, which is the best I’ve tested at its price point.

Sources indicate that the step-down model of our top-rated QM8L, TCL’s QM7L offers many of the same goodies that make its pricier sibling such a rock star, but at a much lower list price. It all starts with the same SQD display tech, for excellent brightness and color vibrancy, and the kind of dimensional contrast that pushes mini-LED closer to OLED.

Industry observers note that the QM7L isn’t quite as much of a powerhouse as the QM8L, but it’s still put-on-your-sunglasses bright, blasting well past anything you can stream, and properly lighting high-quality 4K HDR Blu-rays. Its potency aids in remarkable color expansion for a deep dive into advanced films like Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Importantly, the TV also provides good color accuracy, along with deep black levels for excellent contrast. You’ll still see some minor light bleed if you look for it, and picture quality is reduced off-axis, but both are relatively minor concessions, especially for the price.

Industry observers note that the TV offers a similarly loaded set of gaming features to last year’s QM7K, including options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) across two of its four HDMI inputs. Like the QM8L, its Google TV smart system is intuitive to set up and use. That’s all icing on a TV that comes about as close as I’ve seen to a premium display for the money.

In a recent development, hisense’s mid-tier mini-LED TV doesn’t offer the latest display technologies like RGB LED or Super Quantum Dots, but it does offer seriously punchy performance, along with a design that feels much more premium than its price class suggests. That starts with Hisense’s latest anti-reflective matte screen that eliminates most ambient reflections, matched by slim bezels and a stylish pedestal stand with the kind of build quality usually reserved for flagship TVs.

Under the hood is a potent mini-LED display that employs regular quantum dots for rich colors and brightness that meets or beats anything in its class, including TCL’s QM7L. When paired with its rich black levels and reflection-repelling screen, you’ll have no trouble watching even darker shows in a bright room. Hisense’s image processing has also improved for enhanced detail and upscaling with low-quality content. I did notice that the TV’s local dimming may create some artifacts at its highest setting, but it’s a very minor problem. Like most backlit TVs, it also loses some picture quality when viewed from an angle.

Feature-wise, the U7SG is a gaming master, including VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 165 Hz across all four HDMI inputs, and handy extras like an intuitive game bar for adjusting settings on the fly. Add in its snappy Google TV interface, and you’re getting a whole lot of good stuff at a price that often falls well below $1,000 for a 65-inch model, and stays competitive up to a whopping 116 inches.

After skipping a year, Hisense’s flagship U9 series is back, now loaded with the latest RGB LED display tech for a striking makeover. The TV uses its tri-colored red, green, and blue mini-LED backlighting to great effect, providing rich black levels and sparkling colors that increasingly close the gap with OLED, alongside the kind of dazzling brightness that OLED can’t yet match.

The UR9’s screen gets an advanced version of Hisense’s matte-like anti-glare coating called “Obsidian,” which impressively repels ambient and even most direct light sources, making it a great option in sunlit rooms. Turn the lights off, and you’ll find great shadow detail and very little light bleed from bright objects on dark backgrounds.

Hisense outfits the TV with some premium extras, from a capable 4.1.2-channel speaker system to HDMI 2.1 support at up to 165 Hz across all three HDMI inputs. There’s also a DisplayPort for connecting a PC, though I would have liked to see a fourth HDMI 2.1 port as well. The TV has also gotten an update for the latest advanced HDR format, Dolby Vision 2, making it well-primed for the future. It’s all wrapped in a stylish design, for a posh taste of next-gen luxury at an accessible price point.

According to recent reports, TCL was so confident in its entry-level QM6K that it was the first TV the brand released with its new mini-LED display tech in 2025, and the only major model that wasn’t replaced for 2026. That badge of honor is well earned, as the QM6K is one of the best-performing TVs I’ve tested in its price class, with naturalistic colors, rich black levels and contrast, and enough brightness to properly light up HDR scenes like a blazing sunset or a jet’s afterburners.

Maybe just as impressive are the issues the QM6K avoids. While most TVs in its class readily reveal issues like screen aberrations on solid backgrounds, light bleed from bright images, and awful off-angle performance, the QM6K mostly stays clear of those pitfalls so you can simply enjoy the picture without distraction. My only real performance complaint is the TV’s particularly bad sound, but given that nearly all TVs I test are much better off with a soundbar or speaker system, that’s not a major surprise.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to extras, the QM6K is well stocked with options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz for blur-free action and a gaming bar to adjust features on the fly. And while the TV isn’t nearly as bright as my top budget pick, the U6SF Pro, its Google TV smart system is more intuitive and responsive for a better overall user experience. With a 55-inch model now available for under $500, the QM6K is tough to pass up.

Industry observers note that most TVs on this list are available from 55 inches to large-scale models at 98 inches or larger, and at increasingly reasonable price points. A significant reason for that is, unlike OLED, mini-LED TVs are scalable at a relatively low cost, so screens fit for large home theaters are much more attainable. That’s one of mini-LED’s biggest advantages over other display tech, not to mention the potential for next-gen brightness and color coverage at lower pricing. That said, ultra-large screens more readily expose performance problems, so it’s key to balance screen size with quality so you don’t regret your purchase later.

It has been revealed that all of the TVs on this list offer 4K resolution with HDR (High Dynamic Range), and you wouldn’t want to buy a TV with lower resolution these days unless you’re looking for a very small screen (around 48 inches or lower) for a bedroom or office. The majority of new content is shot in 4K with HDR, the latter of which provides higher brightness and better contrast between the lightest and darkest images, along with the potential for more vibrant colors. Some TVs still offer 8K resolution, but because 8K content is scarce and difficult to recognize with the naked eye, it’s essentially dead (or at least dormant) in the current TV landscape.

As for refresh rates, any TV with 120-Hz or higher is preferred for fast-moving content like sports and, especially, gaming. All of the TVs on this list offer 120 Hz refresh rates or higher with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), designed to adjust to games dynamically to reduce lag and screen tearing/blur. Many TVs push to 144 Hz or better, but those refresh rates are only accessible with select gaming PCs. For consoles—PS5, Xbox Series S/X, and the Nintendo Switch 2—120 Hz is sufficient.

Sources indicate that all of the displays on this list use mini-LED-backlighting, a smaller and more accurate version of traditional LED backlighting, paired with a liquid-crystal display (LCD). Because mini-LEDs are smaller, they can be used more prevalently to create better brightness and more dimming zones, which can enhance black levels for better contrast between the brightest and darkest images. Mini-LEDs can also be enhanced by features like quantum dots, nanoparticles that produce pure bright colors when exposed to light. Some advanced Mini-LED TVs also use RGB LED technology, which trades uniform blue or white mini-LEDs for multicolor red, green, and blue light clusters designed to produce purer, more expansive colors at the light source.

According to recent reports, in contrast (no pun intended), OLED displays use organic material excited by electricity to light each of a TV’s millions of pixels independently. These self-lit (a.k.a. self-emissive) displays have distinct advantages, including the ability to create perfect black levels for enhanced contrast over backlit displays, along with much wider viewing angles. Like mini-LEDs, some OLED displays also use quantum dots: So-called “QD-OLED” TVs offer enhanced brightness and colors, among other fresh technologies to compete with ever-brighter and more advanced mini-LED TVs.

Both display types have their advantages. OLED is the best choice for those after a more balanced, nuanced, and uniform picture, especially if money isn’t a concern. However, because mini-LED is generally cheaper to produce, it may be a better choice for those on a budget who want the largest and brightest screen for their money. And in recent years, the best mini-LED TVs have increasingly advanced to better compete against OLED.

Recent findings suggest that the most crucial connectivity option for gamers is HDMI 2.1, which offers higher bandwidth to get the most out of gaming devices. HDMI 2.1 allows for high refresh rates and features like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) from devices like the PS5, Xbox Series X, and gaming PCs. If you’re only connecting a Blu-ray player or streaming device, HDMI 2.0 will suffice. All of the TVs on this list also support HDMI eARC/ARC, which allows you to easily connect newer soundbars and other audio devices at high resolution for enhanced audio performance.

Sources indicate that wiFi 6 or 7 may also be helpful for wireless streaming, especially if you’re watching a lot of high-resolution content, though you’ll need a router that supports those formats. Most TVs also include an Ethernet connection for a mainline connection to your modem. Other connection options to consider include Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, ATSC 3.0 for features like over-the-air HDR from an HD antenna, and an optical connection for older audio devices like a legacy amplifier or soundbar.

All the TVs on this list come with a smart TV platform for streaming from popular apps, and many include options that let you stream content directly from a smartphone like Apple AirPlay or Google Cast. My favorite platforms are Roku and Google TV, which I find the easiest to navigate and use on a daily basis. All smart platforms collect some form of personal information, so it’s notable to be careful when agreeing to terms and licensing to protect your privacy.

It has been revealed that each TV also supports multiple HDR formats, which is important for getting the best performance. HDR10 is the baseline format, which all modern TVs support. Most TVs also support dynamic HDR formats like Dolby Vision and HDR10+ (many support both). These advanced formats can provide a more precise vision of a director’s intent by adjusting the brightest and darkest images scene by scene, and even frame by frame. Dolby Vision is the most common dynamic HDR format for streaming.

If you’re interested in voice control, you’ll want to look for voice assistants like Roku Voice, Amazon Alexa or Alexa+, and Google Assistant or Gemini. If you’re connecting an audio device that supports spatial audio, like a Dolby Atmos soundbar or A/V receiver, you may also want to ensure your TV supports 3D audio formats like Dolby Atmos and, for 4K Blu-rays, DTS:X.

Ryan Waniata is a professional writer, editor, video host, and product reviewer. A musician since childhood, his audio hardware roots go back to his days as a studio engineer in Nashville, TN in 2009. In 2011 he left the studio world to became a full-time journalist, with an emphasis on A/V, including TVs, speakers, headphones, and audio gear of all kinds. The author of hundreds of articles, Ryan has a passion for finding readers the best value on the best gear out there.

New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov.
  • Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.
  • Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., mentioned he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., mentioned he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune stated of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Industry observers note that sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

According to recent reports, “They got to give us an upgrade,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”.

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly stated legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

In a recent development, duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who stated over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration mentioned Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy mentioned the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

Sources indicate that “In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”.

In a recent development, A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he stated included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”.

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

Sources indicate that “I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune remarked. “We’ll hear him out.”.

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., remarked on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

Poseidon Expeditions has offered an early glimpse into the Ocean Spirit, its purpose-built fresh expedition ship.

Debuting in late 2028, the PC6 class Ocean Spirit is an expedition vessel developed specifically for the cruise line thanks to a deal inked between Poseidon and United Waterways and its ocean division Ocean Advice this summer.

Poseidon has now shared that the 120-meter-long ship will be able to accommodate 160 guests in suites across seven categories: Window, Balcony, Promenade, Deluxe, Captain’s, Panorama and Owner’s.

The suites range in size from 19 to 40 square meters and select categories will feature balconies.

Beyond suites, the ship will feature public spaces designed to complement the journey, including lounges, dining spaces, observation decks and wellness facilities.

Noting that this marks a newly introduced chapter for the firm, the cruise line remarked that the Ocean Spirit carries the ethos of Poseidon Expeditions forward as a new expression of the spirit of exploration that has guided it from the beginning.

Poseidon added that the specifications are preliminary and subject to change.

Latest Update: Do You Trust Your Own Intuition? Here’s How You Sharpen It—And Win at Life, Researchers Say

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • According to recent reports, think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go.
  • Intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, indicates Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

According to recent reports, think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go. In fact, you can hardly explain how you learned in the first place or exactly how you’re keeping your balance as you pedal on. You just trust your body to do it. The same applies to cognitive activities: As a child, you had to really think about how to arrive at the answer of 2+2, but now, you just know it’s four, without thinking.

Intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, indicates Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris. At its core, your intuition is a behavior your brain develops based on patterns and experiences over time, a kind of automation for something you’ve done countless times. That’s why intuition is often linked to expertise. Trusting your gut may sound ill-advised, so why wouldn’t you want to think things through? But it turns out that generating your instincts for decision-making can both help you make the right choice in times of confusion and stress, and also free up mental resources for other tasks.

So, can you train your intuition to sense better choices?

Well, it’s not that simple, according to De Neys, whose research focuses on how intuitive and deliberate thinking develops over our lifetimes. You can’t sidestep the deep reflection needed to build the foundation of your intuitions. But you can tap into them in a more meaningful way, especially over time.

According to recent reports, “Having gut feelings and intuition and even valid intuitions, there’s science to back it up,” De Neys says. “It exists, but it’s always tied to expertise, and expertise means it’s something that you’ve done a lot.”.

Intuition isn’t some overall sense; instead it’s tied to one area of expertise, like an interviewer being able to pick up on the candidate who’ll be the right fit for the job, or an experienced doctor delivering a diagnosis. While you won’t have expert intuition about everything under the sun, there are a few ways you can boost your own decision-making.

First, you need to get better at pattern matching, and that means practice. Intuition is tied to pattern-matching, Jeff Larsen, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains. For example, chess masters earn their distinction by practicing so much that when they see the board, they don’t have to stop and think about what the two or three best moves will be. Others with less expertise may watch a game and think, “that was a silly move,” but they don’t realize the master player has spent years building up pattern recognition, or an accurate gut feeling, Larsen explains.

Industry observers note that second, stop second-guessing your intuition. You can do this by asking yourself, “How might I be wrong?” One approach is to ask a friend who may disagree with you or might have an outside perspective. This can also help you understand that, often, an instinctual choice you made in the heat of the moment is correct. Even if the choice isn’t exactly right, it’s probably good enough to keep you safe. For example, when you’re driving down the interstate, you have some intuition about whether you can make a lane change or not, and whether you need to slow down or speed up to avoid an accident. Thinking about the consequences of your decision-making can also help give you more confidence in your intuition.

Sometimes you have to trust your gut on a truly life-changing decision. When it comes to marriage, the information overload can sometimes feel overwhelming. However, when it comes to close relationships, you’ve presumably experienced many behavioral exchanges with your partner, and this allows for substantial information-gathering to “feed your gut,” Michael Olson, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains.

Recent findings suggest that since you can’t possibly keep this massive load of information in your conscious memory at all times, it translates into a neat summary of all those behavioral exchanges. Now you have a gut feeling that this person is right for you—or not.

Industry observers note that and the research agrees. A study Olson coauthored, published in Science, found that the “explicit,” or “conscious” evaluations couples in the study made of their partners while in the so-called initial “honeymoon stage” didn’t mean as much when stretched over four years. Instead, those who reported positive gut feelings over this time period had a more accurate idea of their happiness in their relationship.

In a recent development, your gut doesn’t just extend to your love life. Trusting it can also help you to be successful in business. Elizabeth Rea, an evidentiary clairvoyant psychic medium, now teaches established founders and CEOs to tap into their own intuitions, through her tech giant, Insightful. As a medium, Rea has also assisted U.S. federal special agents investigating cold murder cases.

When working with clients, she asks them to relax what they consciously believe. Sometimes so-called gut feelings may come to us in the form of chills down our spine or another physical sensation. But since we’re living in a left-brained culture that prizes making decisions using logic and analysis, those instincts often get passed off as coincidences and ignored, Rea says. Sometimes, gut feelings may also be ignored because of self-doubt. Your intuition often whispers to you, she tells clients. Honing these signals will help you improve your self-trust—thereby improving your intuition.

According to recent reports, overall, training yourself to trust your intuition will help you become a better decision-maker. You’ll make the right choices without the agonizing process of picking through pros and cons and running scenarios in your brain for days on end.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s a lot more cost-efficient if we can offload [decision-making] to our intuition,” De Neys claims. “Often that’s going to be helpful because then it frees up resources for something else that might be more notable at that point in time.”.

Oceanwide Sail Expeditions has unveiled that it concluded an expedition that landed guests at the emperor penguin colony on Snow Hill Island.

Guests onboard the Ortelius experienced the northernmost emperor penguin colony on Earth, offering an opportunity to observe adults and chicks.

Following IAATO guidelines, guests observed the colony in an intimate setting.

“This successful landing is a testament to the expertise and dedication of our teams, as well as the remarkable capabilities of the Ortelius,” remarked Remi Bouysset, CEO of Oceanwide Expeditions.

“We are proud to work with some of the very best specialists in the industry, whose experience and professionalism consistently enable us to push the boundaries of polar exploration.”.

The company said in a press release that operating in Antarctica, particularly in the Weddell Sea, requires extensive experience, careful planning and the ability to adapt to constantly changing conditions.

To maximize the chances of reaching Snow Hill Island, Oceanwide incorporated operational flexibility into its expedition planning.

The Ortelius, Oceanwide Expeditions’ ice-strengthened expedition vessel, is purpose-built for exploring some of the most remote and challenging regions on Earth.

The organization added that the ship’s capabilities, combined with the experience and dedication of its crew and expedition team, make it suited to expeditions into the Weddell Sea.

In 2025 and 2026, the ship set a newly introduced farthest south record for a non-icebreaker vessel in the Weddell Sea as part of the firm’s “Remote Weddell Sea Explorer” itinerary, set to return for a final time later this Antarctic season.

Two further In Search of the Emperor Penguin Snow Hill Island itineraries are scheduled in the coming weeks, operated by Oceanwide, with additional landings anticipated later this month and in early December.

The itinerary is set to return in the company’s 2027-28 and 2028-29 seasons.

No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that senate Democratic leader Charles E.
  • ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once remarked.
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once remarked. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”.

Recent findings suggest that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

According to recent reports, now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Recent findings suggest that trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

It has been revealed that voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

According to recent reports, white evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

It has been revealed that if you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

Sources indicate that at the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oceania Cruises has unveiled a new Chef’s Studio aboard the Oceania Marina, introducing a venue for culinary education, destination discovery and chef-hosted experiences at sea.

Beginning November 25, 2026, the venue will welcome guests for a new series of culinary workshops, seminars and test kitchen experiences.

“Since introducing the first hands-on cooking school at sea aboard the Oceania Marina, Oceania Cruises has continually evolved the ways guests can connect with destinations through food and culture,” stated Jason Montague, chief luxury officer of Oceania Cruises.

“The newly introduced Chef’s Studio complements The Culinary Center while offering a different style of culinary enrichment, allowing guests to explore technique and the importance of linking place, history and gastronomy.”.

Debuting following the Oceania Marina’s extensive bow-to-stern refurbishment in October, the Chef’s Studio builds on the ship’s pioneering culinary legacy.

Designed for 18 guests, the Chef’s Studio offers a new perspective on learning opportunities with a roster of seminars, workshops and destination-focused discussions led by Chef Instructors, the manufacturer noted in a press release.

The company stated that the venue’s newly introduced Test Kitchen Series features one-hour classes offered on sea days for $49 per person.

It is designed for travelers seeking a deeper understanding of food and culture.

Sessions focus on techniques and culinary fundamentals with topics ranging from The Spice of Life, knife skills, pantry organization and cooking with high heat to destination-inspired classes exploring regional ingredients, traditions and culinary practices from around the world.

The Chef’s Studio also serves as the gathering place for Oceania Cruises’ signature Culinary Discovery Tours.

According to the press release, guests meet before these small-group tours for an orientation and overview, and once the tour returns, guests and the chef return to the Chef’s Studio for a glass of wine to continue conversations and ask follow-up questions.

In 2027, Oceania Cruises expects to offer more than 100 chef-led Culinary Discovery Tours in destinations spanning Iceland, Australia, Uruguay and beyond.

The Chef’s Studio program will expand next year and debut aboard the Oceania Riviera and the line’s latest additions to the fleet, the Oceania Sonata and Oceania Aurelia.

#31295. Industry News: How to Plan a Trip to the World’s Largest Ski Resort, Les Trois Vallées

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2103 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How to Plan a Trip to the World’s Largest Ski Resort, Les Trois Vallées

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Standing at the top of a steep gully, I looked down at the line ahead.
  • Recent findings suggest that before I dropped in, I looked out at the view ahead.
  • Les Trois Vallées (also known as Les 3 Vallées, or the 3 Valleys) began with the construction of a 19-passenger open-air “chairlift” in 1938 in the small town of Méribel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Standing at the top of a steep gully, I looked down at the line ahead. A handful of tracks cut through 10 inches of powder to my left, telling the story of the skiers who arrived before me. But I couldn’t help but notice untouched snow under an overhanging cliff face to my right.

Recent findings suggest that before I dropped in, I looked out at the view ahead. I could make out tiny chairlift towers on the snow-capped peaks and ridgelines on the horizon. It felt as if the entire mountain range belonged to the Les Trois Vallées Ski Resort, one of the best—and the biggest—ski destinations in Europe.

Les Trois Vallées (also known as Les 3 Vallées, or the 3 Valleys) began with the construction of a 19-passenger open-air “chairlift” in 1938 in the small town of Méribel. But it wasn’t until 1971, with the creation of the joint ski pass that offers access to the seven resorts that make up Les Trois Vallées, that the ski area took its current form.

Today, the resort spans three main valleys and has 169 chairlifts accessing nearly 26,000 acres of skiable terrain (for comparison, Park City has 7,300 acres of skiable terrain). That makes it the world’s largest interconnected ski area—and it’s all accessible via a single ski ticket. Lift tickets for each of the seven resorts are available, but the cost savings don’t make it worthwhile—for a couple of extra euros, you can buy a pass that gives you access to the entire resort. Les Trois Vallées is also a convenient destination for Epic Pass holders, who get seven days of skiing at Les Trois Vallées.

Given the destination is so vast, here are some tips for navigating the expansive terrain and various villages that make up Les Trois Vallées, based on my most recent trip in 2026.

An aerial view of the skiing area of Les Trois Vallees, also known as The 3 Valleys.

In a recent development, “We need to ski over there today,” our guide and former ski racer, Timothée “Timy” Theaux, notes as he pointed toward a distant ridgeline. “The wind is coming from Italy, so that side of the ridge is where we’ll find the best snow.”.

We skied seamlessly from lift to lift until we reached an open bowl with untouched powder. Theaux knew exactly where to go given the current conditions, and how to get there.

Industry observers note that les Trois Vallées isn’t like a typical US resort. The terrain is so vast and complex that skiing it without a guide can be more of a chore than skiing with one. Guides—which you can hire through each resort’s ski school, like ESF Val Thorens—not only know how to navigate the resort and keep you safe off-piste, but also know exactly where to go to score skiers the best possible conditions and overall experience.

I pictured myself without a guide at the resort, spending day after day staring at trail maps, hopping on lifts that dropped me a mile from where I thought they would. Thankfully, our guide’s expertise spared us from what could’ve been a logistical nightmare.

Industry observers note that on our third day at the resort, low visibility made it hard to see more than 15 feet ahead. As we impatiently waited for the fog to lift, lapping groomed runs outside of our hotel, Theaux decided to head toward Courchevel.

“Courchevel and Méribel are good to ski when visibility is low,” he told us, explaining that they’re both at a lower elevation and have more tree skiing.

Recent findings suggest that even if it’s just for a day or two, hiring a guide at the beginning of the trip will help skiers and riders get a feel for Les Trois Vallées and each individual resort. While all seven resorts offer a good mix of terrain for every ability level, some, like Val Thorens, sit at a higher elevation and have more alpine terrain than resorts like Courchevel, which are lower and have more tree skiing.

Sources indicate that the terrain is also so vast that it’s not hard to avoid crowds—which typically stick to the pistes at each resort (Courchevel, Val Thorens, and Méribel are some of the more popular ones). Focusing on one resort per day, rather than spending an entire day riding lifts from one side of the resort to the other, is a stellar way to maximize time on snow.

Backcountry skiers can enjoy the vast off-piste areas beyond the resort's groomed runs.

According to recent reports, unlike many US ski areas, there aren’t dedicated off-piste areas marked on a map—everything within (and really, outside of) the resort’s boundaries is fair game. But leaving the pistes requires a guide, or at the very least, knowledge of how to navigate backcountry terrain. A low-angle, mellow backcountry slope can rapidly steepen enough to raise avalanche concerns, and skiers who leave the pistes should be able to recognize and manage backcountry hazards. And while not all off-piste terrain at Les Trois Vallées requires the chops of an expert skier, it doesn’t take much to get yourself in trouble. When it came to navigating the resort, keeping us out of trouble, and scoring the best conditions away from the crowds, Theaux took out all of the guesswork.

After several lift rides and traverses, we finally found ourselves in Courchevel, on the opposite side of the resort from where we were staying in Val Thorens. We immediately left the groomed runs and headed for the trees, leaving the crowded pistes behind.

As a Latest Englander, I feel at home in tight, scrappy tree runs. But leaving the pistes to explore the vast terrain and significant lines encompassed by Les Trois Vallées was special. Unlike the runs I’ve grown accustomed to at my local ski areas, pistes at Les Trois Vallées don’t have a hard line defined by thick trees and icy trail edges; almost everything is skiable.

“Dropping into an off-piste line alone, with just your guide, is one of the most special feelings in the world,” says Dan Egan, a pro skier who has been spending winters in France for nearly three decades. He was skiing with us for the week. “You really get to connect with the place in a way you never would on a groomed run filled with people.”.

It has been revealed that at the top of nearly every chairlift, I spotted about a dozen distant backcountry lines I wanted to explore. Saw-toothed peaks gave way to steep chutes and couloirs, many of which funneled into open powder fields. “I need to come back and ski that,” I found myself thinking about a dozen times per day.

Courchevel is perhaps the spiffiest resort at The Three Valleys—but there are budget-friendly villages nearby.

In a recent development, each resort town has its own feel, so it’s key to know your priorities before booking. Courchevel, for example, is the most luxurious destination, while Col de la Chambre is perfect for skiers who want to spend their evenings partying. Budget-conscious skiers should consider Brides-les-Bains or Orelle; whereas Les Menuires might be better for families. Saint-Martin and Méribel both have a cozy European village vibe, but Méribel might have the slight advantage for off-piste skiers.

Val Thorens is known for its vibrant aprés-ski scene.

According to recent reports, when we first arrived at the Fahrenheit Seven hotel in Val Thorens, I felt like I was in an early 2000s ski movie. The back deck was packed shoulder to shoulder, and the DJ knew just what to play to keep the crowd going. It was the middle of the afternoon on a random Sunday.

Industry observers note that while there is plenty of partying to be done all over Les Trois Vallées (the parties at La Folie Douce Val Thorens and La Folie Douce Méribel are not to be missed), there are also more laid-back places to stay. Of the seven resorts and villages, each has its own unique feel and caters to different types of skiers. And all of them offer lift access to the pistes.

In a recent development, “Courchevel is my favorite place to ski because it has a lot of luxury restaurants and accommodations, so hardcore skiers think it’s not for them,” Theaux told us during our low-visibility day. “The off-piste terrain is always empty.”.

But if you’re heading to Courchevel for the accommodations over the skiing, Les Airelles Courchevel is about as luxurious as it gets.

According to recent reports, saint-Martin-de-Belleville, slightly below Val Thorens in the Belleville Valley, has the quiet feel of a quaint European hamlet. Like Val Thorens (and most villages around the resort), it’s very walkable, but it's better for skiers who value history and culture over parties. Orelle, made up of 10 hamlets and less popular than other villages, and Brides-les-Bains, known for its thermal waters and spa culture, are also quiet options; the latter is great for budget-conscious travelers.

In a recent development, méribel, next to Courchevel's high-end restaurants and parties, is known as a family-friendly resort village with plenty of restaurants, bars, shops, and easy lift access. Similarly, Les Menuires is also known as a family destination, but is ideal for skiers looking to explore some of Les Trois Vallées’ bigger off-piste terrain.

Food across the resort is locally sourced, even at on-hill dining options, like Caron 3200.

No matter which village you stay in, good food is never more than a couple of steps or a chairlift ride away.

“I really love the jamon because it requires patience,” says Vincent Suchet, the cheesemaker and grandson of Pépé Nicolas at family-owned, Michelin-starred Chez Pépé Nicolas—located just below Val Thorens in the Belleville Valley. He told us as we sipped wine and tasted local cheeses in a cool, stone-walled cellar: “And I favor the cheeses because you have to wait two years; the flavor is the best when you have to wait.”.

It has been revealed that the culinary experience stood in stark contrast to what I was used to at US ski areas—fast service, overpriced, yet mediocre cheeseburgers and pizza, and ingredients sourced hundreds, if not thousands, of miles away. At Les Trois Vallées, home to ten Michelin-starred restaurants like Hotel La Bouitte, the food is just as notable as the skiing.

Industry observers note that during my week at the resort, I couldn’t find a single fast-food or chain restaurant in any of the seven villages. Restaurants are all family-owned, and thought goes into where ingredients are sourced. It’s not uncommon for cheeses to be made by a local farmer whose family has been doing it for generations.

Caron 3200, perched above Val Thorens, is the highest wine bar in Europe.

Even on-hill dining options, like Caron 3200, perched above Val Thorens at 10,500 feet (making it the highest wine bar in Europe), emphasize the culinary experience.

According to recent reports, “We have 150 different wines, and most are French,” Eric Bonnel, managing director of Val Thorens Tours, told us as we sipped wine and admired the views of Mont Blanc and the surrounding Alps through the oversized windows. “And we store them at three different altitudes. The reds are aged at a higher altitude because there’s less oxygen.”.

According to recent reports, on our last evening at Les Trois Vallées, it finally started snowing. I momentarily felt a slight sense of disappointment about leaving ahead of a huge storm. But as I sipped my post-meal Génépi with newly introduced and old friends, I realized it didn’t matter. The skiing was only a small part of the Les Trois Vallées experience.

Les Trois Vallées is accessible via train, plane, or car.

It has been revealed that for international travelers, the most convenient airport to fly into is Geneva, which is located just a couple of hours from the resort (depending on where you’re staying). While the Swiss airport has the most international flight options, it’s also possible to fly into Lyon, Chambéry, and Grenoble.

In a recent development, companies like Alpine Fleet offer shuttle transfers from the airports to the resorts in Les Trois Vallées. You can also rent a car, but with the lifts and shuttles available in each resort town, you don’t really need one once you arrive.

Those traveling within Europe or from one of the area’s international airports can access Les Trois Vallées by train, with the Moûtiers﻿ train station serving major cities like London, Paris, Geneva, and Lyon. From the train station, travelers can get to each resort by taxi or bus.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Marella Cruises is expanding its regional flying program for the winter season, enabling guests to spend Christmas holidays sailing the Caribbean while flying from Newcastle.
  • Thanks to a direct TUI Airways flight to La Romana, Dominican Republic, departing Newcastle Airport on December 15, 2026, guests can sail a 14-night Caribbean fly-cruise that combines the “Colors of the Caribbean” and “A Caribbean Christmas” itineraries aboard the Marella Discovery.
  • They can also prolong their stay by combining the “Colors of the Caribbean” itinerary with a one week stay post-cruise at a choice of TUI hotels in La Romana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marella Cruises is expanding its regional flying program for the winter season, enabling guests to spend Christmas holidays sailing the Caribbean while flying from Newcastle.

Thanks to a direct TUI Airways flight to La Romana, Dominican Republic, departing Newcastle Airport on December 15, 2026, guests can sail a 14-night Caribbean fly-cruise that combines the “Colors of the Caribbean” and “A Caribbean Christmas” itineraries aboard the Marella Discovery.

They can also prolong their stay by combining the “Colors of the Caribbean” itinerary with a one week stay post-cruise at a choice of TUI hotels in La Romana.

“We’re delighted to be expanding our regional flying program from Newcastle Airport for Winter 2026, giving customers across the North East even more choice when it comes to starting their Caribbean holiday closer to home,” stated Chris Hackney, CEO at Marella Cruises.

“Regional flying is incredibly important to us at Marella Cruises and the additional La Romana flying means customers can enjoy the convenience of departing from their local airport before experiencing everything our all-inclusive cruises and cruise and stay program has to offer.”.

The itinerary sailing roundtrip from La Romana calls at Roseau, Dominica; St John’s, Antigua; Basseterre, St Kitts; Philipsburg, St Maarten and Road Town, British Virgin Islands during the first week.

The second week visits Isla Catalina, an island off the Dominican Republic; Kralendijk, Bonaire; Willemstad, Curacao; Oranjestad, Aruba before returning to La Romana.

Prices start from £2,868 per person, based on two adults sharing a balcony cabin.

Leon McQuaid, director of aviation development at Newcastle Airport, noted: “Spending Christmas in the Caribbean is on many people’s bucket list, so it’s fantastic that passengers can make that dream a reality with direct flights from Newcastle Airport.

“Marella Cruises’ expanded program makes it easier than ever to swap the cold winter weather for Caribbean sunshine and stunning beaches, while exploring the region’s most spectacular islands.”.

Breaking: Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress.
  • As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.
  • Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she stated, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Industry observers note that her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her newly introduced colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”.

Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” stated Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan mentioned.

According to recent reports, as returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

Not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” remarked Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number mentioned otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat presently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

It has been revealed that “If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira remarked. “This is low on my priority list.”.

Some members announced their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

Sources indicate that “First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” remarked Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” remarked Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”.

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he said of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

How I Got My Visa to France

📅 16 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010.
  • In a recent development, but that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées.
  • Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand demonstrated me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

In a recent development, but that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”.

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.).

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:.

Sources indicate that the student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is at the moment there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

Recent findings suggest that but this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

It has been revealed that additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you strategy to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

Recent findings suggest that so I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It has been revealed that it’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

According to recent reports, my biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office mentioned last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

Recent findings suggest that but does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

Industry observers note that the gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

It has been revealed that for this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this organization, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.).

According to recent reports, the main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:.

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment mentioned the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

Industry observers note that the worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.).

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

According to recent reports, so, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other complications or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!
