Tech Report: 21 Best Places to Visit in December in the USA

📅 31 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theplanetd

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we’ll never forget the first time we visited Newly introduced York City in December.
  • Recent findings suggest that but December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa.
  • In fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we’ll never forget the first time we visited Newly introduced York City in December. We’d seen it in movies, but standing there, seeing the Rockefeller Center tree all lit up for the first time, with skaters below and festive music in the air… it was pure magic.

Recent findings suggest that but December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa. We’ve also spent the holidays escaping to the warmth, trading snow boots for flip-flops.

In fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather. We’ve done so many road trips in the USA and flown almost everywhere, trying to find the best places to either escape the snow or enjoy the winter, you would think we are obsessed. And we want to share all of that knowledge with you.

If you’re looking for the perfect winter getaway, you have a clear choice: either lean into the winter magic or escape it completely. Are you dreaming of a warm-weather escape with sunshine and sand, or a storybook Christmas town that looks like a real-life snow globe?

In a recent development, based on all those experiences, we’ve put together this list of our favourite places to visit. Whether you’re looking for a festive city, a snowy mountain, or a sunny beach, we’ll help you find the perfect spot.

Here is a quick look at some of the best places for a December getaway in the USA, from festive winter wonderlands to sunny escapes.

According to recent reports, december is a month of pure magic and festive energy. It’s the perfect time to use up that last bit of vacation time for the year. The biggest draw is the distinct choice it offers: You can either dive head-first into a winter wonderland, complete with snow and holiday markets, or you can completely escape the cold weather and find yourself on a sunny beach. It’s a month of festive celebrations, incredible decorations, and finding the perfect atmosphere to end the year.

Industry observers note that if you’re anything like us, sometimes the best gift in December is a break from the cold. Trust us, we know after living in Toronto, Canada. Those winters are brutal. These are our favourite spots to find sunshine and warm weather, where you can trade your winter coat for a light jacket or even a swimsuit.

We love the laid-back, quirky vibe of Key West, and it’s even more special in December. We have a great memory of biking around the island, seeing the historic inns draped in holiday lights, and then ending the day at Mallory Square for the sunset celebration. It’s a perfect escape from the cold.

Why Visit in December: This is the perfect time to visit. The summer humidity is gone, the weather is sunny and warm (often in the high 70s), and the risk of hurricanes is very low. The whole island is in a festive spirit, with unique events like the “Bight Before Christmas” boat parade.

Where to Stay: We recommend finding a guesthouse or inn in the historic Old Town to be close to the action.

It has been revealed that we once went to a holiday luau in Ka’anapali, and it’s an experience we’ll never forget. You’re eating kalua pork and sipping a mai tai, watching a beautiful hula performance… and then Santa Claus arrives on an outrigger canoe. It was the perfect, uniquely Hawaiian way to get into the festive spirit.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: You get tropical weather, festive holiday luaus, and it’s the official start of the humpback whale watching season. Be aware that this is a popular time, especially around Christmas, so prices can be high and you’ll need to book in advance.

Where to Stay: Look to the resorts in Wailea or Ka’anapali for a classic Maui experience.

According to recent reports, we’ll always remember snorkeling the underwater trail at Trunk Bay in St. John. The water was so calm and clear, and seeing all the colourful fish felt a world away from the snow back home. That’s the magic of a Caribbean trip in December, and the USVI makes it so easy for American travelers.

Why Visit in December: It’s the start of the dry season, with fantastic weather and warm, clear water. You get a full-on tropical, warm-weather Christmas experience, all without needing a passport.

According to recent reports, where to Stay: You can choose from large resorts in St. Thomas or more eco-friendly villas and lodges in St. John.

Sources indicate that we were not prepared for how magical St. Augustine is in December. We took one of the Old Town trolley tours at night, and seeing the entire historic city, from the old Spanish architecture to the palm trees, draped in millions of white lights… it was breathtaking. It’s a holiday light display unlike any other.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: The famous “Nights of Lights” festival. The entire city is illuminated, and the mild Florida weather is perfect for walking around and enjoying the atmosphere. It’s one of the most festive and warm places you can visit.

Where to Stay: We recommend a historic inn or bed & breakfast in the downtown district to be within walking distance of all the lights.

Sources indicate that while Maui is our go-to for a resort escape, Honolulu is where you go for a vibrant, city-meets-beach holiday. We loved seeing the massive Santa surfing with his reindeer in the fountain at the Iolani Palace. The whole city has this amazing “Mele Kalikimaka” (Merry Christmas) spirit.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect blend of warm beach weather, world-class shopping, and festive displays. It’s also a significant month for history, with the memorial events at Pearl Harbor.

Where to Stay: Waikiki has a huge range of hotels, from historic beachfront properties to modern high-rises.

If your idea of a winter getaway is to truly get away from everything, the crowds, the noise, the stress, then South Padre is a perfect choice. We spent a week there, and our days consisted of long, quiet walks on the beach. It was a total reset and the perfect way to escape the winter blues.

Why Visit in December: The weather is mild, and the crowds are gone. It’s one of the warmest places in Texas and offers a simple, relaxing beach vacation without the high prices or holiday chaos of other destinations.

Where to Stay: You’ll find many beachfront condos and hotels offering great off-season rates.

According to recent reports, we thought we knew desert holiday lights, but the “Las Noches de las Luminarias” at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix is on another level. Walking the garden paths lit by thousands of hand-lit luminaria bags, with musicians playing, was a top-tier holiday experience.

Why Visit in December: You get two trips in one: perfect, sunny weather for outdoor adventures like hiking during the day, and stunning, sophisticated holiday light displays at night.

Where to Stay: Choose from upscale resorts in Scottsdale or stylish hotels in downtown Phoenix.

In a recent development, sometimes, the warm weather destinations just won’t cut it, especially if you are looking for that winter wonderland feel. So, this section is for travellers who want to dive head-first into the holiday spirit. These are the cities and towns that go all-out for December, with millions of lights, Christmas markets, and an atmosphere of pure magic.

According to recent reports, we’ve visited NYC many times, but there’s a specific energy in December. We grabbed hot chocolates and walked through the Bryant Park Winter Village, watching the ice skaters zip around the rink under the lights of the surrounding skyscrapers. It felt like being in the opening scene of a holiday movie. There is nothing like New York City at Christmas.

Sources indicate that why Visit in December: It is the quintessential American Christmas destination. From the iconic tree to the world-famous window displays, the entire city is on a different level of festive.

Where to Stay: Midtown is convenient for seeing the main holiday sights, but we also love the West Village for its cosy, neighbourhood feel.

Industry observers note that we’d heard Leavenworth was a “Christmas Town,” but we weren’t prepared for the reality. We visited during the Village of Lights festival, and walking through the snow-covered Bavarian-style village while every single building was covered in over half a million lights… it’s not an exaggeration. It’s the closest we’ve ever felt to being inside a real-life snow globe.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: The entire town transforms into a “Hallmark movie” Christmas village. It’s a full-immersion holiday experience with carolers, festive food, and incredible decorations.

Where to Stay: Book a Bavarian-style lodge or inn right in the village. You must book many months in advance for December.

According to recent reports, we love Asheville, but visiting in December is all about the Biltmore Estate. We took the candlelight evening tour, and seeing the main banquet hall with its 35-foot tree, fireplaces roaring, and carolers singing… it felt like we’d stepped back in time into a Gilded Age Christmas party.

Why Visit in December: Christmas at Biltmore is one of the most iconic holiday events in the country. The city itself is a cosy mountain retreat, and the Blue Ridge Mountains are just beautiful with a dusting of snow.

Where to Stay: You can stay on the Biltmore Estate for the full experience or choose a boutique hotel downtown.

Here are the remaining destinations for the “Best Christmas Towns & Festive Cities” section, all written with unique, December-focused content.

Sources indicate that we’ve visited a lot of Christmas markets, but visiting the one in Bethlehem, known as “Christmas City USA”, just felt right. We sipped hot cider and browsed the stalls in the old quarter, and you can feel the city’s 250+ years of Christmas tradition. The whole place is lit by the glow of a giant Moravian star on the hillside.

Why Visit in December: This is Christmas City USA. It was nicknamed this on Christmas Eve, 1741. It offers one of the most authentic and historic holiday experiences in the country, blending its Moravian heritage with a European-style Christkindlmarkt.

Where to Stay: Look for a hotel or inn in the historic downtown area to be close to the festivities.

Sources indicate that walking into Solvang in December felt like we’d been transported to a Danish village during its Julefest celebration. We spent the day exploring the half-timbered buildings, windmills, and bakeries, all decorated for the holidays. It’s such a unique and charming way to experience a winter getaway in the middle of California.

Why Visit in December: The town’s month-long “Julefest” (Yule-fest) celebration is in full swing. It’s a one-of-a-kind Danish-style Christmas with parades, markets, and, of course, delicious European pastries.

Where to Stay: Choose one of the charming Danish-themed inns right in the village to be in the middle of the Julefest activities.

Industry observers note that we had to see the “Christmas Capital of Texas” for ourselves, and it did not disappoint. The entire historic Main Street is transformed. We loved seeing the vintage railroad, which becomes the “North Pole Express” for the month. They take the “Christmas Capital” title seriously; there are over 1,400 events in 40 days.

Why Visit in December: It is the officially designated “Christmas Capital of Texas”. The sheer number of festive events, light displays, and activities is staggering, making it a top-tier destination for families and holiday lovers.

Where to Stay: The Gaylord Texan Resort is an attraction in itself, or you can stay near the Historic Main Street to be close to the events.

A New Orleans Christmas is an experience all its own. We did a “Reveillon Dinner,” a modern take on a Creole holiday tradition, and it was one of the most memorable meals we’ve ever had. Afterwards, we walked to Jackson Square to see the St. Louis Cathedral all lit up while carolers sang.

Sources indicate that why Visit in December: You get to experience unique Creole Christmas traditions you won’t find anywhere else. The weather is mild, the food is incredible, and the city’s lobbies (like at The Roosevelt) have some of the most elegant decorations we’ve seen.

Where to Stay: We recommend a hotel in the French Quarter to be in the middle of the action and see the decorated lobbies.

It has been revealed that we went to Natchitoches (pronounced Nak-a-tish) specifically for its Christmas Festival, and it was a total joy. It’s one of the oldest and biggest in the country. The whole city, which is the oldest in Louisiana, lights up with over 300,000 lights along the Cane River, and the weekly fireworks shows are fantastic.

Why Visit in December: It hosts one of the oldest and most celebrated holiday festivals in the US, running for six weeks. It’s a classic, Southern Christmas experience in a beautiful historic district.

Where to Stay: Book a room at a historic bed & breakfast in the downtown area.

Visiting Colonial Williamsburg in December felt like walking through a living history Christmas card. We joined a candlelight tour, and seeing the historic buildings lit by real candles in the windows, with carolers in period costumes and the smell of woodsmoke in the air… it was absolutely magical.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: You get to experience a traditional, 18th-century “Colonial Christmas”. The decorations are all-natural (no plastic lights), and the atmosphere is incredibly authentic and charming.

Where to Stay: Stay in one of the historic Colonial Houses or a tavern right in the restored area for the full immersive experience.

Sources indicate that here is the final category of destinations. This section is all about embracing the snow and finding that perfect winter wonderland.

According to recent reports, for many, holiday season travel is all about finding that perfect, snowy scene. These are the places to go for world-class skiing, cosy lodges, and that magical feeling of a true winter escape.

Industry observers note that we’ll always remember our first “après-ski” in Aspen. We had spent the day on the mountain hitting fresh powder whenever we got the chance, and as the sun went down, the sky lit up with this incredible pink and orange light they call “Aspenglow.” Sitting by a fire, enjoying a glass of Christmas cheer, and watching the snow fall on the historic town, it just felt like the peak of a luxury winter trip.

Industry observers note that why Visit in December: It’s one of the world’s most famous upscale ski destinations, and the town is just as much an attraction as the mountains. The festive atmosphere, high-end shops, and restaurants are all decked out for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Aspen is known for its luxury hotels and ski-in/ski-out resorts.

According to recent reports, one of our favourite things about Park City is its history. We loved skiing down to the historic Main Street, popping off our skis, and walking straight into a saloon that’s been there since the silver mining days. It feels like a real Western town, not just a ski resort.

Industry observers note that why Visit in December: It’s a historic mountain town with two world-class ski resorts (Park City and Deer Valley). The historic Main Street is incredibly charming, and the “Snow Globe Stroll” features life-sized snow globes you can walk through.

Where to Stay: You can find ski-in/ski-out hotels or stay at an inn on the historic Main Street.

Jackson Hole in December is just dramatic. We took a sleigh ride through the National Elk Refuge, and seeing thousands of elk gathered against the backdrop of the snow-covered Teton mountains… it was a powerful and wild winter experience we’ve never forgotten.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect mix of rugged “cowboy Christmas” charm and some of the most challenging ski terrain in North America. The town square, with its famous antler arches, is beautifully lit for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Stay at a slopeside resort in Teton Village or in a hotel in the town of Jackson.

We love Whitefish because it feels like a real, down-to-earth ski town. We spent a day snowshoeing in nearby Glacier National Park, enjoying the total silence and incredible snowy landscapes, and then came back to town for a casual dinner. It’s all the beauty, without the glitz. Just what we were looking for in a winter vacation.

Why Visit in December: It’s a laid-back, charming mountain town with a top-rated ski resort and stunning scenery. It’s also right next to Glacier National Park, which is a spectacular place to explore in the winter.

Where to Stay: You can find lodges on the mountain or stay in one of the friendly inns in downtown Whitefish.

In a recent development, this was a trip purely for the fun of it, and it was 100% worth it. You drive down streets named “Santa Claus Lane” and “St. Nicholas Drive,” the streetlights are shaped like candy canes, and you can visit the Santa Claus House and see his reindeer. It’s a surreal and joyful experience.

Why Visit in December: It’s the ultimate Christmas fantasy come to life. The entire town is Christmas-themed, 365 days a year, but it’s most magical in December with real snow on the ground and the added bonus of possibly seeing the Northern Lights.

Where to Stay: North Pole is very small; most visitors stay in the nearby city of Fairbanks, which has a wide range of hotels.

According to recent reports, for the best warm weather, your top choices are Southern Florida (like Key West), Hawaii (like Maui and Honolulu), and the desert Southwest (like Phoenix and Palm Springs). The U.S. Virgin Islands are also a fantastic passport-free tropical option.

Industry observers note that leavenworth, Washington, is often considered the ultimate “Christmas town” as it looks just like a Bavarian snow globe. Other top choices include Bethlehem, PA (known as “Christmas City USA”), Solvang, CA (for a Danish-style Julefest), and Grapevine, TX (the “Christmas Capital of Texas”).

Recent findings suggest that yes, but it depends on the park. It’s the perfect time to visit desert parks like Death Valley, Everglades, and Substantial Bend, where summer heat is unbearable. However, many mountain parks like Glacier, Yellowstone, and parts of Yosemite are mostly inaccessible due to heavy snow and road closures.

Industry observers note that you are almost guaranteed to find snow in the mountain towns of the Rockies, like Aspen, CO, Park City, UT, and Jackson Hole, WY. You’ll also find snow in the Cascade Mountains (like Leavenworth, WA), Alaska, and the mountains around Lake Tahoe.

According to recent reports, december is a magical month to travel. Whether you’re chasing the sun, seeking out that perfect snowy scene, or looking for a town that’s full of holiday magic, the US has the perfect spot for you.

We hope this list, based on our own winter travels, helps you plan your next getaway. Save this on Pinterest for your holiday planning! Where is your favourite place to go in December?

The Best Places to Go in Central and South America 2027

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is my fourth year leading our guide to the Best Places to Go in Central and South America, and each time I’m in awe of the final result—our list for 2027 is no exception.
  • It may be a fool’s errand to distill all this wonder into a list of just 10 destinations.
  • These are the Best Places to Go in Central and South America in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is my fourth year leading our guide to the Best Places to Go in Central and South America, and each time I’m in awe of the final result—our list for 2027 is no exception. We’re talking about a region where the Pacific, the Atlantic, and the Caribbean converge; where the Andes reach for the Amazon; and where strings of puffy volcanoes and postcard-worthy islands stud the map like jewels. Within it all there are thriving cities where cultures ancient and modern collide head-on, and small towns that are timeless in a way that feels increasingly rare.

It may be a fool’s errand to distill all this wonder into a list of just 10 destinations. But the places below, as singular or more broadly representative as they may be, are the region’s answer to how we are traveling right now. For example, a pioneering set of travel specialists are ready to bring you to eco-lodges that are tucked in the untamed jungle of Guyana for wildlife sightings and citizen science experiences that will broaden your understanding of the only (official) English-speaking country in South America. If you’re looking for a sport to pick up, Preá on Brazil’s northeast coast has an open invitation on kitesurfing, the wind-driven sport this fishing village has long been known for—and the reason a set of quietly luxurious boutique hotels have been cropping up within driving distance of the rolling sand dunes of Jericoacoara National Park. If wine is what moves you, then Chile’s Central Valley should be your next stop: A slew of latest culinary experiences and interesting bottles from up-and-coming winemakers make this Santiago-adjacent region the trip to take in 2027. There’s also next-gen wellness in Costa Rica, quintessential expedition cruises in Ecuador, offseason trekking in Argentina, and so much more.

Get ready to max out that PTO. These are the Best Places to Go in Central and South America in 2027. —Megan Spurrell.

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: upcoming jungle stays, ancestral wellness experiences, and a next-level approach to ecotourism.

Tucked in the Monteverde Cloud Forest, Hotel Belmar's Artista Villas offers 10 bungalows in a reforestation site.

The chance to connect with nature has long been a draw to this region—at Hotel Belmar, that includes activities like yoga.

Half a century ago Costa Rica helped pioneer a fresh model of travel in the Monteverde Cloud Forest that would come to be known as ecotourism. Today the free-spirited residents of Monteverde, three hours northwest of the capital, San José, are once again redefining responsible travel—yet now the goal extends beyond minimizing tourism’s footprint to actively restoring ecosystems, supporting local communities, and forging deeper connections between visitor and place. That ethos is embodied by Artista Villas, a collection of 10 swish bungalows in a reforestation site at Hotel Belmar. Guests at the carbon-neutral property, which opened in June, engage with the surrounding jungle using in-room art kits, meet visiting artists and filmmakers at the property’s Cervecería Belmar, forest bathe in the mountain at Artista-owned Savia nature reserve, and learn about the source of their meals at Finca Madre Tierra. Calling this new form of regenerative travel ecotourism feels too small to capture its weight.

As conventional foreign-owned resorts proliferate along the nearby Gulf of Papagayo, Monteverde and the surrounding highlands continue to chart a different course. In March 2027 the working ranch and private reserve Hacienda Montezuma, located beneath the Tenorio Volcano (and normally reserved for exclusive buyouts), will launch the first in a series of wellness retreats bookable for up to 15 people. These will feature local practitioners leading equine therapy, meditation, and forest walks—all rooted in ancestral traditions. The region is also transitioning to a deforestation-free coffee model that is reshaping how one of Costa Rica's most vital crops is both grown and experienced by visitors on educational tours. —Mark Johanson.

Go for: chef-led experiences, upcoming Cachapoal Valley bungalows, and up-and-coming wine scenes.

In Chile's best winemaking regions, there's plenty of old and upcoming. Case in point: Chile’s most extravagant wine hotel, VIK, expanded in 2026 with eight glass-mirrored bungalows and an art-filled wellness center, with five cabins set to open next in an oak forest on the property.

Chile’s central wine valleys have long been defined by their vines—emerald rows sprawling along riverbanks, blanketing a terrain reminiscent of the Mediterranean, yet hemmed between towering Andes and a thrashing Pacific. Recently, dynamic chefs from Santiago have begun adding their touch to the region, crafting new culinary tours and elevating the work of emerging bodegas and wineries. Kurt Schmidt is among them. He first rose to fame crafting nine-course tasting menus at Santiago’s 99 Restaurante, built around the traditional foodways of Chilean viticultural regions. In 2027 he’ll be teaming up with the rural tourism cooperative Ruta de los Abastos (“The Supply Route”) on menu-to-territory day tours that will begin at 99 and expand out to wine valleys like Huasco, Maule, and Aconcagua, where Schmidt has spent years building relationships with vintners, cheesemakers, foragers, and fisherfolk (later multiday itineraries are in the works). Conveniently, Santiago lies just south of the Maipo Valley, which is famed for bold Cabernet Sauvignons and also home to the striking new Centro del Vino from Concha y Toro, Latin America’s largest wine producer. The 129,000-square-foot facility features contemporary art installations, barrel-side tasting rooms, and an interactive wine museum, plus access to manicured gardens and (for an additional fee) the 19th-century mansion of founder Don Melchor.

Industry observers note that if you have days to spare, consider heading three hours south to the Cachapoal Valley. Here, Chile’s most extravagant wine hotel, VIK, expanded in 2026 with eight glass-mirrored bungalows and an art-filled wellness center. Five cabins are next, set to open in an oak forest on the property, where winemaker Cristián Vallejo ages natural wine in clay amphorae. Continuing south, you can explore the next generation of experimental and low-intervention vino emerging from the neighboring Maule and Itata valleys, where Millennial and Gen Z winemakers are injecting fresh energy into one of South America's oldest regions at bodegas like González Bastías and Carter Mollenhauer. Add it all up and it makes for an epic wine country road trip.

Sources indicate that as if that weren’t enough to keep you busy, know that excellent vino isn’t the only reason to dedicate your substantial vacation to Chile this year. Once you wrap up in Santiago, consider hopping over to Rapa Nui (Easter Island) for some extreme set-jetting. This remote Chilean territory in the Southeastern Pacific is the backdrop of Academy Award winner Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, and it’s sure to become a rising star on more travelers’ itineraries this year. —Mark Johanson.

Go for: newly introduced conservation-minded cruises, stargazing experiences, and an endless parade of wildlife.

In 2027 National Geographic–Lindblad Expeditions will celebrate 60 years since Lars-Eric Lindblad introduced travelers to the Galápagos on the first nonscientific civilian expedition voyage, establishing the islands as a premier destination for conservation-minded exploration.

The Galápagos Islands, an archipelago of 13 major isles and over 100 rocks and inlets off Ecuador’s coast, have long attracted travelers seeking solitude and wildlife: endemic giant tortoises and marine iguanas, native scalloped hammerhead sharks, and blue-footed boobies, for starters. Nearly 97% of the Galápagos’ land area is a single national park. Visitor access remains tightly managed, making the destination one of the rare places where travelers can experience wildlife on nature’s terms (and, as scientists are learning, occasionally encounter latest species, like the deep-sea Microeledone galapagensis, or blue octopus). In 2027 National Geographic–Lindblad Expeditions will celebrate 60 years since Lars-Eric Lindblad introduced travelers to the Galápagos on the first nonscientific civilian expedition voyage, establishing the islands as a premier destination for conservation-minded exploration. The brand doubled its Galápagos fleet in 2025 by adding the 16-guest catamaran Delfina and the 48-guest Gemini. In January 2027 the brand will launch Ultimate Galápagos, a 13-day itinerary aboard the 96-passenger Endeavour II that visits 11 islands including remote Genovesa, known for its red-footed booby colonies. Elsewhere, Natural Habitat Adventures’ Galápagos Tortoise Camp just transitioned to 100% solar power and introduced the Galápagos’ first fully electric panga (a small skiff for excursions)—part of trips booked aboard the brand’s Petrel luxury catamaran—reducing emissions for wildlife excursions and setting a new benchmark for sustainable travel in the destination. —Hannah Selinger.

Go for: volcano trekking, peak birdwatching, price points that range from shoestring to major spender.

Guatemala, beloved for its artisan heritage, birdwatching, and volcano trekking up peaks like the Volcán de Fuego (pictured), will continue to draw a wide range of travelers in 2027.

Long a backpacking destination on the Central America 101 route known as the Gringo Trail, Guatemala is an increasingly popular destination for a generation of young travelers seeking slower, more enriching tourism that won’t break the bank. INGUAT, the Guatemala Institute of Tourism, notes that arrival numbers support the TikTok thesis—and are only projected to increase. Some of the appeal is timeless: Guatemalan day-to-day life is deeply steeped in ancient heritage and culture. Sprawling artisan markets like Nim Po’t in Antigua offer easy access to hand-carved and painted wood animal masks, for example, but deeper dives are offered by Antigua-based textile studio Luna Zorro, which organizes craft retreats throughout the country. The brand’s recently opened La Valiente (February 2026) is a two-bedroom guesthouse in the heart of the city, and almost everything at the property—from the bedding to ceramics—is artisan-made by local creators. The country’s natural beauty is also an evergreen draw, but as younger generations embrace the mores—and aesthetics—of hiking (and even birdwatching), trails like the rigorous two-day Acatenango trek are list-toppers in the central highland region that is ripe with some of the 780 species recorded in Guatemala. Many choose to continue to the Tikal National Park in the northeast, where 3,000-year-old ruins of the Maya city sit amid a lush green jungle setting. At the park’s recently reopened Conservation and Research Center, visitors can observe the behind-the-scenes preservation process of ruins and artifacts, only now visible to the public. It all makes for welcome news that Guatemala is getting even easier to access: Frontier is offering daily, seasonal, nonstop service from Los Angeles to Guatemala City from December 17 until January 4, if you need a last-minute holiday getaway, and United Airlines has a permanent direct route from Houston. —Anna Zou.

Go for: untamed rainforest, immersive eco-lodges, and easier-than-ever access.

Guyana still remains 85% forested, with sites like the impressive Kaieteur Falls—among the world's strongest single-drop waterfalls—awaiting travelers.

Guyana, South America’s only country with English as its official language, celebrated six decades of nationhood this May. Yet from a small plane bound for Kaieteur Falls, one of the most powerful single-drop waterfalls in the world, the lush rainforest below appears several geological eras older. Perhaps it’s no wonder; an impressive 85% of this country remains forested.

Sources indicate that most travelers start in the coastal city of Georgetown, where the country’s Caribbean identity is tangible in the annual Mashramani carnival (every February), vibrant Stabroek Market, and Gothic St. George’s Anglican Cathedral, which is made of wood. But journeys swiftly turn toward the rainforest and savanna, with Kaieteur as their most dramatic introduction. At the falls, the Potaro River drops 741 feet from a sandstone ledge—more than four times Niagara’s height—yet just over 8,000 people see it each year, usually on a day flight from Georgetown. A fuller interior journey requires a separate, multiday circuit through Iwokrama International Centre for Rainforest Conservation and Development (IIC), a nearly million-acre reserve managed alongside 20 Indigenous communities, and into the North Rupununi, a landscape of savanna, wetlands, and river villages where Indigenous-led conservation becomes part of the itinerary. For in-the-know travelers, right now—when a host of fresh expeditions and accommodations have risen to meet vanguard voyage interest—is the time to go.

On that circuit, three conservation-linked stays give travelers a direct role in the work. Atta Rainforest Lodge is the base for Iwokrama’s canopy walkway, suspended 100 feet above the forest floor and managed by the reserve in partnership with Makushi communities and local tourism operators. Further into the North Rupununi, road and river lead to Rewa Eco-Lodge, operated by Rewa Village, where anglers help measure and tag arapaima before release. Another tributary leads to Yupukari’s Caiman House, a village-run guesthouse and research station where visitors help researchers study black caiman after dark. The community also raises yellow-spotted Amazon river turtles for release. Reaching these stays still requires small planes and long road-and-river transfers, though one important link is easing: In August 2026, Jags Aviation added a 19-seat turboprop service four days a week between Georgetown’s Eugene F. Correia International Airport and Lethem.

Back in Georgetown, the arrival of international hotel brands marks a new era at the start and finish of any trip. The 152-room AC Hotel opened in December 2025, with the 172-room Four Points by Sheraton following in April 2026. A Hilton resort is due on the seafront in 2028. And there are more reasons to linger in 2027: From October 8 to October 17, the capital will also host Carifesta XVI, which will return the Caribbean Festival of Arts to its 1972 birthplace, promising a cultural counterpart to the wilderness of the interior. —Paul Jebara.

Go for: new off-season expeditions, and a slate of fresh lodges.

For the first time in 2026, tour company Hielo & Aventura offered its popular ice hiking excursion atop the Perito Moreno Glacier—in winter.

It has been revealed that los Glaciares National Park, with its toothy granite spires, windswept steppe, and glaciers that crack and roar as they calve into milky-blue lakes, has long been the crown jewel of Argentine Patagonia. Yet its main gateway town, El Calafate, hasn’t seen a latest luxury hotel in over two decades. That changes in December 2026 with Explora El Calafate, an all-inclusive 20-key lodge snaking across a Patagonian estancia near Lake Argentino. The hotel’s design leans into soothing earth tones—with giant windows framing distant glaciers—while menus highlight Patagonian lamb, trout, and wine. Guides take guests on 30 different adventures out to remote wildlands like the ice fields of Brazo Sur or the bird sanctuary of Laguna Nimez. Explora will simultaneously open a second property just across the Chilean border in its private Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve, further linking the two destinations by building out a binational circuit.

In a recent development, meanwhile, southern Patagonia is shedding its reputation as a summer-only destination. Awasi Patagonia, near Torres del Paine, will now remain open through the 2027 winter season—prime time for puma safaris—while ecotourism operator Chile Nativo extols the virtue of the offseason with its Winter W Trek, tracing the iconic route past Paine Grande and the Grey Glacier in the region’s quieter season. The momentum is even greater in Los Glaciares. In 2026 park concessionaire Hielo & Aventura, responding to greater off-season demand that can help disperse the annual tourist traffic, operated its popular ice hiking excursion atop the Perito Moreno Glacier during the winter for the first time. Unlike most Patagonian mountain towns, El Calafate doesn’t shut down when crowds depart, which means there are still hot chocolates to be had after a day on the ice. —Mark Johanson.

Go for: a buyout villa in jaguar country, and groundbreaking conservation efforts.

Caiman’s new private villa, Cordilheira, has seven bungalows with buyout options for larger groups, offering a new way to stay in this wildlife-rich corner of Brazil.

It has been revealed that for flora and fauna lovers headed to South America, the Amazon has long been the marquee trip. But further south, where the waters of the Amazon trickle down into the world’s largest tropical wetland, something different awaits. The Pantanal stretches across 42 million acres in Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay. In comparison to the Amazon, it’s a bit more arid, with strong cowboy culture, and the foliage is sparser, making this a great place to spot jaguars in the wild. This is in no small part thanks to notable conservation work that has taken place over decades. At the upscale Caiman Pantanal, a trailblazing safari stay in the Brazilian Pantanal, jaguar rescue group Onçafari has an on-site location, allowing guests at the all-inclusive property to explore 131,000 acres of land with the major cat experts who have meticulously tagged and tracked dozens of them. Caiman’s latest private villa, Cordilheira, was unveiled in June 2026. It brings together seven bungalows (private infinity pools included) that fit up to 16 people, making it possible for families and groups to have a buyout experience as they spend days tracking jaguars—and tapirs, and giant anteaters, and capybaras—before evenings filled with Brazilian barbecue and folk music under the stars. Operators like Natural Habitat Adventures can continue the journey northbound to destinations like Porto Jofre, where cat sightings happen by boat on the river, and jaguars can be seen chasing caimans at the water’s edge. The conservation work required to protect this rare natural landscape and its fauna is ongoing, but new projects like the Jaguar Rivers Initiative, unveiled in fall 2025, prove the only way is forward. This new coalition, which connects the aforementioned Onçafari with Kristine Tompkins’s Fundación Rewilding Argentina, Nativa in Bolivia, and Fundación Moisés Bertoni in Paraguay, hopes to better link and restore various jaguar habitats. The goal is, of course, ecological first and foremost—but if the preservation work in Pantanal has taught us anything so far, it’s that great conservation can lead to great wildlife experiences. —Megan Spurrell.

Go for: uncrowded surf spots, a noteworthy beach hideaway, and plenty of seafood.

Opened in February 2026, resort Inkaterra Cabo Blanco overlooks the Pacific Ocean on a coastline frequented by Marilyn Monroe and Ernest Hemingway.

The seaside towns and villages of Peru's northern shore are known for their seafood dishes, such as picante de mariscos and raw-fish tiraditos.

Sources indicate that on Peru’s northern coast, life moves slowly in the seaside towns and fishing villages that have long drawn a quiet trickle of visitors including surfers chasing mythical waves, Limeños lured by closer-to-the-equator sun and tranquility, and culinary-minded travelers who know that nowhere else does seafood quite like this part of the country. In the past few years, an increasingly stylish crop of Airbnbs have popped up—like Kahu Beach House in Los Órganos, where modern design uses endemic natural materials and where fantastic surf breaks are visible from your breakfast table. The more recent resort opening of Inkaterra Cabo Blanco in February 2026 has shone an even brighter spotlight: On the same stretch of sand where Marilyn Monroe and Ernest Hemingway vacationed in the 1950s, this contemporary beachside stay with just 13 rooms is an elegant approach to the destination’s barefoot ease, refined coastal dining, and experiences that range from a day on the water with a local fishing collective to surfing and kitesurfing lessons just steps from the private plunge pools. (Editor's note: The resort is temporarily closed due to El Niño rains.) As for the region’s culinary offerings? You won’t have to look hard. This sun-baked stretch of coast is where carne seca dries on clotheslines and makes its way into seco de chavela (a pounded beef and plantain dish bursting with chile), and where Peruvian classics like conchas a la parmesana (scallops baked with cheese) are remixed using conchas negras, a unique shellfish found in the mangroves of Tumbes, near the border with Ecuador. Hearty dishes like picante de mariscos, a seafood stew, sit side by side with chilled raw-fish tiraditos that fly close to the sun in their spice. —Megan Spurrell.

Go for: kitesurfing for pros—and newbies—in a fishing village now home to quietly luxurious stays.

With the charm of a fishing village and powerful winds, Preá has become an ideal kitesurfing destination.

From spa treatments to horseback riding and yoga Preá's hotel scene brings a bevy of activities to travelers.

Preá has the unmistakable charm of a Brazilian fishing village—a seemingly endless shoreline, a sandy-street village center, and beachfront restaurants serving fresh-caught seafood—with one major difference: wind, and lots of it. From July through early January, this sleepy town catches some of the world’s most consistently powerful gusts, the kind kitesurfers cross oceans for. Now, with the sport growing in popularity, beginners are starting to come too, bringing with them an exciting upcoming energy. Kitesurfing has become so popular among Brazil’s well-heeled travelers that Marco Dalpozzo, a partner at the pioneering pousada Rancho do Peixe, dubbed the sport “the new golf, the new tennis, the new skiing.” Learning takes some commitment: First-timers start on the sand before progressing into the water, with a full beginner course happening over several days. Yet new kitesurfing locations are making it easier than ever for newcomers to join the scene.

Recent findings suggest that while the famed Jericoacoara next door is known for its lively nightlife and parties, Preá’s new crop of high-end boutique hotels and villas offers a more exclusive take on barefoot luxury. Think ocean-facing rooms, intimate private villas, and seaside bungalows paired with their own kite schools, full-service spas, and feet-in-the-sand restaurants. Whether you’re up for braving the wind or not, there is plenty else to do in terms of both adventure and restorative wellness.

It has been revealed that preá offers easy access to the landscapes that made neighboring Jericoacoara famous. Set off by buggy or quad to explore the region’s enormous sand dunes and freshwater lagoons that naturally occur between them, or visit the otherworldly Jericoacoara National Park. Back in Preá, book a treatment at L’Occitane spa at the Preabeach Boutique Hotel, take advantage of the yoga offerings at Hotel Kabana, or horseback ride along the shore. By sunset, everyone gathers on the beach to watch the last kiters streak across the water as what looks like a giant ball of fire slips into the ocean. Later, dinner can range from candlelit seaside dining to charming restaurants like Casinha in the rustic village center, where flip-flops are acceptable attire.

Industry observers note that the wind is bringing in major investments too. Grupo Carnaúba is building what it envisions as the wind sports equivalent to an Alpine ski resort. Its members-only Carnaúba Wind House, opened in 2024, offers bungalow stays with a kite center, beach club, restaurant, and freshwater lagoon, while the larger Vila Carnaúba development is adding more luxury residences and beach tennis facilities. The biggest arrival yet comes in 2028, when Anantara opens its first property in the Americas: A beachfront resort complete with its own signature spa and dedicated kitesurfing school. —Carla Vianna.

Go for: cheffy restaurant openings, a revitalized downtown, and a lineup of literary festivals.

Bachour by Mata (above) is pastry chef Antonio Bachour's first Latin American pastry shop—and it joins a wave of buzzy culinary openings that have made this city an increasingly hot food destination.

São Paulo is a city for those with an appetite—for business, culture, and, of course, food. Brazil’s largest and most frenetic metropolis is home to some of Brazil’s most extraordinary architectural landmarks, from Lina Bo Bardi’s museum of art (MASP) to Paulo Mendes da Rocha’s reimagined Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo. Meanwhile, the restaurant landscape has never been more exciting: São Paulo is now home to the only two restaurants in the Southern Hemisphere recently awarded three Michelin stars: Tuju and Evvai.

That momentum is reshaping the city well beyond its established dining districts: Near Avenida Paulista, the Mata São Paulo hospitality complex has gathered some of the city’s buzziest names, including Mata Città, Korean barbecue spot Lavva, and pastry chef Antonio Bachour, who opened his first Latin American pastry shop Bachour by Mata here, all in one place. More is on the way, including a new boteco, Á Brasileira, from Janaína Torres (named the World’s Best Female Chef in 2024 by World’s 50 Best). Her beloved Bar da Dona Onça, on the ground floor of Oscar Niemeyer’s sinuous Copan building, has itself gained new neighbors, including seafood-focused Brisa do Barú and Tem Umami!, an ice cream shop with a near-permanent line out the door. Together with an observation deck, the new arrivals are turning the 1,160-apartment Modernist landmark into one of downtown’s liveliest destinations.

Also inside the Copan is Livraria Megafauna, part of a new wave of independent bookstores bringing literary life back to São Paulo’s streets. Its Poesia no Centro poetry festival, returning in April 2027, has already become a fixture on the city’s cultural calendar; meanwhile the growing Feira do Livro, organized by literary magazine Quatro Cinco Um, is expected to draw around 100,000 people to the Praça Charles Miller in May 2027, and it will nearly double the space devoted to its mostly independent publishers.

That literary boom is part of a broader cultural surge, with major events like SP-Arte in April and the Bienal de São Paulo—Latin America’s largest visual arts event—returning to Ibirapuera Park in September. The expansion of Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand, the city’s landmark art museum, only adds to the momentum: Its newest building, opened in March 2025, increased exhibition space by more than 60% and made room for upcoming highlights and works from the collection previously kept out of public view. —Rafael Tonon.

Industry News: Airport Luggage Tag Scam: How to Protect Your Checked Bags in 2026

📅 14 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theplanetd

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine walking up to customs after a long international flight and being told that a suitcase connected to your name has been flagged.
  • Then the officer points to the luggage tag and indicates, “Then why is your name on it?”.
  • Recent findings suggest that that is the nightmare behind a luggage scam travelers need to understand in 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine walking up to customs after a long international flight and being told that a suitcase connected to your name has been flagged.

Then the officer points to the luggage tag and indicates, “Then why is your name on it?”.

Recent findings suggest that that is the nightmare behind a luggage scam travelers need to understand in 2026. It is called baggage tag switching, and it is exactly what it sounds like: the luggage tag from an innocent passenger’s checked suitcase is allegedly removed and placed onto another bag.

According to recent reports, baggage tag switching scams happen when the luggage tag from a traveler’s checked bag is allegedly removed and placed on another suitcase. To protect yourself, take a video of your suitcase before check-in, photograph the bag on the scale, take a close-up photo of the baggage tag, keep your baggage receipt, place a tracker inside your suitcase, and report any damaged, missing, delayed, or retagged bag before leaving the airport.

According to a W5 investigation, innocent passengers flying from Canada have been detained after their real luggage tags were allegedly moved onto suitcases containing illegal drugs. The investigation focused on flights from Canada and alleged cases connected to Toronto Pearson, but the larger lesson applies to travelers everywhere: once your checked bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting the system to protect your luggage, your tag, and your name.

According to recent reports, we have traveled to more than 130 countries on all seven continents, and checked bags have always been part of travel. But the old habit of simply handing over your suitcase and hoping for the best needs an update.

In 2026, protecting your checked luggage is not just about stopping theft. It is about protecting the paper trail that connects you to your bag.

This is part of a bigger shift in how travelers need to think about airport safety, baggage scams, and common airport security mistakes before they fly.

Editor’s note: This article is based on our video about baggage tag switching, which has reached more than 86,000 views on our travel YouTube channel.

Before you check a bag, take two minutes to create proof that the bag is yours.

It also helps to run through a full pre-travel checklist before you leave for the airport so you are not rushing through check-in.

Recent findings suggest that this may sound like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes at check-in. And those two minutes could matter if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

We covered this luggage tag scam in detail in the video below, including the simple two-minute routine we now recommend before checking a bag.

Baggage tag switching is when the tag printed for your checked luggage is removed from your actual suitcase and attached to another bag.

When you check luggage, the airline prints a baggage tag that usually includes your name, flight, destination, routing information, barcode, and bag number. That tag is the airport system’s way of connecting that suitcase to you.

The problem is that once your bag goes behind the counter, you cannot see what happens next.

In the alleged scheme reported by W5, corrupt baggage or ramp workers could remove a legitimate tag from a passenger’s suitcase and attach it to another suitcase heading to the same destination. If that second bag is intercepted, the paperwork points back to the innocent passenger.

In a recent development, that is what makes this scam so dangerous. You may have done everything right: checked your own suitcase, kept your boarding pass, and boarded your flight. But behind the scenes, one strip of paper may now connect your name to a bag you have never seen.

According to recent reports, most airport workers are honest. Let’s be clear about that. The vast majority are doing hard jobs under pressure, moving thousands of bags through complex systems every day. But a baggage system only needs a few bad actors to create a very serious problem.

This story has received attention because of Canadian cases, but this is not only a Canada problem.

The bigger problem is that every major airport has the same basic weak point: you hand over your suitcase, it enters a restricted area, and from that point on, you are relying on the system to protect the tag, the bag, and the records connected to your name.

According to recent reports, that is true in Toronto. It is true in New York, London, Paris, Dubai, Bangkok, Mexico City, Sydney, and anywhere else checked luggage moves behind the scenes.

International travel also adds another layer of risk. If your name gets tied to a suspicious bag in another country, you may be dealing with a different legal system, different customs procedures, and possibly a language barrier.

It has been revealed that the Government of Canada warns travelers that drug offences abroad can have serious consequences and that you should never carry anything across a border for someone else. The Canada Border Services Agency also specifically reminds travelers that trafficking cannabis or other drugs across the border is a criminal offence and warns people to beware of anyone asking them to carry something.

In a recent development, that is why documenting your own luggage matters. You are not being paranoid. You are creating a simple evidence trail.

Before your suitcase disappears behind the counter, take a clear video of it.

Do a full 360-degree view. Show the front, back, sides, wheels, handles, color, brand, straps, stickers, scratches, dents, or anything that makes your bag identifiable.

Yes, you may feel ridiculous filming your suitcase at the airport. Do it anyway. People film lattes. You can film the thing that might keep you out of a holding room.

According to recent reports, this video creates a time-stamped record of what your suitcase looked like before it left your hands. If someone later claims a different bag is yours, you have proof of what your actual luggage looked like at check-in.

When your bag is placed on the airline scale, take a quick photo or video showing the weight.

According to recent reports, this matters because weight is part of the paper trail. If your suitcase weighed 19 kilograms at check-in and another suitcase connected to your name weighs 32 kilograms, that difference may matter.

You are not trying to become a detective. You are simply creating a record that notes this was your bag, this was the weight, this was the condition, and this was the tag attached to it.

That is the kind of simple documentation that can help if your bag is delayed, damaged, retagged, or questioned later.

Once the airline attaches the baggage tag to your suitcase, take a close-up photo or video of it before the bag goes onto the conveyor belt.

Industry observers note that make sure you can clearly see the barcode, destination airport, flight number, routing, and bag number. Also check that the airline has looped and attached the tag properly.

You are not being difficult. You are checking the one strip of paper connecting you to your luggage. That little tag is doing a lot of legal heavy lifting.

Air Canada’s own baggage information explains that self-service kiosks can print baggage tags, receipts, and boarding passes, and that travelers then attach the tags and proceed to bag drop. That means passengers are often handling or reviewing this paperwork themselves before the bag disappears into the system.

Never throw away the little baggage receipt sticker you receive at check-in.

Keep it somewhere safe. Don’t stuff it in a random pocket, lose it before boarding, or assume the airline app is enough. Put it with your passport or travel documents until your suitcase is back in your hands.

Sources indicate that that receipt usually contains your bag number. If something goes wrong, that number becomes part of the evidence trail. That number can help airline staff or investigators compare what you checked, what arrived, and whether someone intercepted or retagged another bag.

This is one of the easiest travel habits to fix, and it costs nothing.

Before you close your checked bag, take one clear photo of the inside.

Recent findings suggest that you do not need to photograph every sock like you are filing a museum inventory. Just take one clear photo of the contents: clothes, shoes, toiletries, chargers, jackets, and the usual chaos of travel.

This helps show what you actually packed. If a suitcase connected to your name contains items you have never seen, you have a record of what was inside your real bag before check-in.

This is especially useful on international trips, where proving what you packed may become more complicated once you are outside your home country.

It is also a good reminder to double-check what not to pack in checked luggage before you leave for the airport.

A luggage tracker will not stop someone from tampering with a baggage tag, but it can help show where your real suitcase went.

We use Apple AirTags, but there are also Tile trackers, Samsung SmartTags, and other luggage tracking options.

In a recent development, the important thing is this: put the tracker inside your suitcase. Do not hang it outside where it can easily be removed.

If authorities are asking about a suitcase connected to your name and your tracker shows your actual suitcase is somewhere else, that becomes another part of your evidence trail.

Recent findings suggest that trackers are also helpful if your bag arrives late, gets separated from its original tag, or ends up in the wrong baggage area. They are not perfect, but they give travelers one more layer of information when airline systems fail.

Sources indicate that we use AirTags in our checked bags, but Samsung SmartTags and Tile trackers are also good options depending on your phone. The key is to keep the tracker inside the suitcase where it cannot easily be removed.

We also recommend pairing a luggage tracker with a few simple anti-theft travel accessories especially on longer international trips.

A plain black suitcase is basically the airport version of camouflage.

Make your luggage easier to identify with a bright strap, ribbon, sticker, or distinctive luggage tag. You want to be able to spot your bag rapidly and prove what makes it different from hundreds of others.

According to recent reports, but do not put too much personal information on the outside. Your name and phone number are enough.

You do not need your home address waving around the baggage hall like an invitation that claims, “Please rob us while we’re in Italy.”.

Keep luggage identifiable, but not overly revealing.

This rule has always mattered, but it matters even more now.

Never carry a package, gift, suitcase, envelope, or item for someone else. That means no favors for strangers, no “harmless” packages, and no quick airport errands for someone you barely know.

If you did not pack it, you do not carry it.

The CBSA specifically warns travelers to beware of people who ask them to carry anything and notes that consequences for drug trafficking can be serious in Canada and abroad.

That is the cleanest rule in travel: your bag, your responsibility.

If your checked bag arrives without the original tag, with a damaged tag, with a rush tag, or through a different baggage process than expected, do not just shrug and leave the airport.

Do not rely on a quick conversation at the counter. Conversations disappear the second you walk away. Written reports create a record.

This matters if your bag was mishandled, delayed, retagged, or separated from its original tag.

When your suitcase comes out at baggage claim, do not grab it on autopilot and leave.

It has been revealed that we have seen people accidentally walk away with someone else’s luggage. It happens more easily than people think, especially after long-haul flights when everyone is tired and half the carousel is filled with identical black suitcases.

Before you leave the airport or customs area, take one minute to confirm everything looks right.

For a smoother trip overall, our easy air travel tips can help before you even reach baggage claim.

For longer flights, our long-haul flight tips can also help make the journey easier before you even get to baggage claim.

The old way of checking luggage was simple: check the bag, keep the receipt somewhere, and hope for the best.

It sounds like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes — and those two minutes could make a huge difference if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

If authorities ever question you about a suitcase that you do not recognize, stay calm.

Do not guess, don’t joke and do not become argumentative.

Ask for legal assistance and show the documentation you collected: your suitcase video, scale photo, baggage tag photo, receipt, tracker information, and photos of what you packed.

This article is not legal advice, but from a traveler’s perspective, the goal is simple: create proof before there is a problem.

If your name is ever attached to a bag you did not pack, your documentation may help show what your real suitcase looked like, what it weighed, what was inside it, and where it went.

Before every checked bag disappears behind the counter, take two minutes to create a simple record of your suitcase.

That’s it. Two minutes. No drama. No paranoia. Just smart travel.

Most airport workers are honest, and most checked bags arrive without a problem. But airport systems are massive, complicated, and not completely invisible-proof. Once your bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting a chain of people, machines, tags, scans, and systems to keep your suitcase connected to your name.

That is usually fine — until it is not.

It has been revealed that so before your next flight, take two minutes to protect yourself. Film your bag. Photograph your tag. Keep your receipt. Use a tracker. And never carry anything for anyone else.

Because when travelers get smarter, scams get riskier for the people trying to pull them off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health initiative, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

The travel insurance firm Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just debuted what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

It has been revealed that nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single plan. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

Sources indicate that but who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really quickly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

For those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the strategy can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

It has been revealed that income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

Sources indicate that if you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

Sources indicate that health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Sources indicate that payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

Recent findings suggest that for health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This latest Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025.
  • Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.
  • The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister presently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a recent development, in a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke remarked.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Concern One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” remarked Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he remarked, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

In a recent development, zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

Recent findings suggest that it marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with intends to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services firm Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

It has been revealed that supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a manufacturer registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

Sources indicate that SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron noted.

In a recent development, since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s firm, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he noted, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail remarked about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.
