    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    In a recent development, the Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    In a recent development, that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an vital part of it.”.

    According to recent reports, “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” stated Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley noted that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley noted. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox mentioned in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    Recent findings suggest that “We require age checks for chat, place customers under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson stated. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a firm’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    Industry observers note that myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She stated Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also stated that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The more we learn about the nationwide FAA ground stop, the less convincing the effort to blame old equipment and previous administrations becomes.
    • A CNN investigation describes a troubling gap between the oversight the FAA indicates occurred and what sources say actually happened.
    • According to recent reports, the problem concerns work by L3Harris at a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, before the November 13 ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The more we learn about the nationwide FAA ground stop, the less convincing the effort to blame old equipment and previous administrations becomes. New reporting points to an oversight policy changed under the current administration and a technician whose role apparently ended after letting a contractor through the door. Aging infrastructure required careful management. Instead, we appear to have received less of it.

    A CNN investigation describes a troubling gap between the oversight the FAA indicates occurred and what sources say actually happened.

    According to recent reports, the problem concerns work by L3Harris at a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, before the November 13 ground stop. According to CNN, an FAA technician provided access to the building but understood that his responsibility ended there.

    One source described the technician this way:.

    “He was only there to unlock the door…there was no monitoring.”.

    Recent findings suggest that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had remarked the installation was monitored. An agency spokeswoman subsequently explained:.

    “The escort is not there while the technician is doing work”.

    Sources indicate that those accounts require reconciliation, but strike me as irreconcilable. Opening a door and overseeing an installation are very different responsibilities.

    A March 2025 FAA memo changed the process for contractor maintenance. Work previously submitted as requests requiring approval became notifications that could proceed without affirmative FAA approval. The policy retained a review role for FAA liaisons, but a small group was tasked with handling thousands of notifications.

    The FAA disputes that the policy reduced oversight, but the questions remain:.

    Recent findings suggest that this is why I find the continuing effort to blame Biden or Buttigieg so absurd. Neither man was running the department when this policy changed or when this installation occurred. I have already written about the contractor questions surrounding this failure. The upcoming reporting makes those questions more urgent.

    Decades of deferred investment explain why modernization is necessary. They do not excuse weakening the supervision of the modernization itself. If anything, working with old infrastructure should make the government more careful about introducing upcoming equipment, not less.

    The staffing matter deserves scrutiny too, also highlighted by One Mile At A Time.

    In February 2025, the FAA fired hundreds of probationary employees during the administration’s government-cutting campaign. Duffy said no controllers or critical safety personnel were among those dismissed. The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union later declared the reinstatement of the 132 terminated employees it represented.

    Sources indicate that that means we cannot necessarily a direct causation from those firings to this outage, though the broader approach remains fair game. An administration that celebrates eliminating positions needs to account for the work those people perform. If that work still needs doing, someone else must absorb it, a contractor must perform it, or it goes undone, a particular concern at an agency already struggling with staffing.

    Sources indicate that in its statement on the ground stop, PASS says the FAA’s May 2026 workforce plan called for at least 750 additional certified professional technicians by 2030. The union says little progress has been made toward hiring them.

    It has been revealed that we can certainly agree that unnecessary government spending should be eliminated. But a smaller payroll does not demonstrate greater efficiency if the remaining organization cannot adequately supervise the work entrusted to it…the cost of a nationwide aviation disruption must enter that calculation too, especially now.

    Meanwhile, Musk is distancing himself from the political movement he helped finance.

    Speaking at the DealBook Summit on November 18, he stated:.

    He described himself as politically moderate, rejected blind adherence to Republican policies, and expressed regret over his election spending:.

    “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it”.

    We joke about United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby adjusting his political posture with the prevailing winds. Apparently, he has manufacturer. I would welcome a sincere reassessment from Musk. But distancing himself from a label does not erase his role in promoting the administration or DOGE.

    It also does not establish that he now recognizes the problems with the personnel policies he championed. Regretting an unsuccessful political investment is different from regretting how the government was managed. Still, when even Musk wants distance from MAGA, I think it is fair to ask whether the brand has reached its expiration date.

    My reading of the election is that Americans are tired of the performance. They want competent government and explanations they can believe. Being told that every success belongs to the president while every failure belongs to his predecessor wears thin and it goes well beyond right/left or Republican/Democrat divisions.

    In a recent development, to be fair, Bedford has now offered something we have heard too little of. As ABC News reports, he noted Wednesday:.

    “I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So blame me. If we need to blame somebody, blame me.”.

    Sources indicate that I appreciate that. He also promised a transparent accounting of the technical findings. But accepting blame must lead to an explanation of the decisions that preceded the failure. It cannot simply shield Duffy or end the inquiry.

    The incoming Congress should audit the maintenance policy, staffing records, risk assessments, and contractor communications. It should establish what oversight was required, what actually occurred, and whether the agency had enough qualified people to carry out its responsibilities.

    Duffy wants another $50 billion. Perhaps the modernization program needs that money. But Congress should understand how the existing process failed before assuming that a larger appropriation will fix it…and maybe remind Duffy that instead of going on reality TV road trips he should have done the job he was hired to do.

    Industry observers note that accountability must become something more useful than another round of political theater that both sides use to score political points. Trump remains president for two more years. The newly introduced Congress will have to work with him to repair the damage and modernize this system.

    Sources indicate that I find his vindictiveness and self-absorption deeply troubling. In his recent 60 Minutes interview with Ross Douthat, he said:.

    “I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”.

    That is a miserable disposition for governing a country whose citizens will always disagree. Even so, waiting for him to become a different person is not a strategy. Congress should pursue practical agreements that restore adequate staffing and contractor oversight while funding necessary upgrades.

    In a recent development, if Trump needs to claim credit for a functioning aviation system, let him. I care far more about the result than denying him another chance to stoke his vanity. Congress can scrutinize the administration’s failures while negotiating legislation that begins to correct them. If the goal is to make things better, then we need to borrow the line from Ronald Reagan: “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.”.

    The latest reporting points toward an oversight failure under the current administration. The exact technical cause and the contribution of staffing decisions still require investigation, but blaming old equipment is plainly insufficient.

    Recent findings suggest that modernizing a system this complex will involve difficulties. I would be much more understanding of an administration that acknowledged those difficulties, explained its mistakes, and corrected them. Instead, passengers have received conflicting accounts and political blame. The latest Congress needs to insist on answers, then work with the president on repairs that outlast the next news cycle.

    Americans need to be able to trust the people running their aviation system…to some extent, the past is in the past and today is a new day and a chance for course correction.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’m standing atop a spit of land jutting out into the English Channel, peering down at a beach accessible only by boat, where a small group of sunbathers lounge on the rocky sand.
    • I was nearing the end of the first day of a three-day solo walking trip along a slice of England’s South West Coast Path, a 630-mile trail through some of the country’s most beautiful land- and seascapes.
    • Since tackling an admittedly easier two-day walk from Dover to Sandwich the previous summer, I’d become totally enamored with England’s coastal paths.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’m standing atop a spit of land jutting out into the English Channel, peering down at a beach accessible only by boat, where a small group of sunbathers lounge on the rocky sand. The view is a welcome excuse to catch my breath before continuing along five more rolling cliffs—400 steep feet up, 400 steep feet down, and repeat. And so, despite my exhausted legs and the blister that’s forming over my right major toe, I decide to imprint this impossibly peaceful scene into my brain to remind myself why I’m doing this trip.

    Dorset's limestone Jurassic Coast.

    I was nearing the end of the first day of a three-day solo walking trip along a slice of England’s South West Coast Path, a 630-mile trail through some of the country’s most beautiful land- and seascapes. Earlier this year, it became part of the newly created King Charles III England Coast Path, inaugurated with a brisk March walk by the king himself (wearing a suit, natch). The route now incorporates all of England’s preexisting regional coastal paths, adding newly introduced sections to create a wider network that stretches across nearly 2,700 miles, giving walkers a chance to access parts of the country far beyond the typical travel itinerary.

    Since tackling an admittedly easier two-day walk from Dover to Sandwich the previous summer, I’d become totally enamored with England’s coastal paths. I realized I could experience so much more of the country’s most beautiful landscapes by foot than I ever could by train or car. For my second foray, I chose one of the more frequented set of trails: walking east from Weymouth to Bournemouth across Dorset. This stretch is known for its incredible rock formations, the result of millions of years of waves washing against the coast. That erosion has also led to the discovery of some of the world’s oldest fossils—giving the region the name of Jurassic Coast.

    A view of the South West coast Path's rugged countryside, which is now more easily accessible to hikers thanks to the wider newly created King Charles III England Coast Path.

    When I’d set off five hours earlier from the charming seaside town of Weymouth—a destination made popular by King George III’s multiple visits at the turn of the 19th century—the going had been easy. My only roadblock was a military parade that a British historical society couldn’t have arranged any better: an Army band marched in front of a stretch of beach-facing Georgian townhouses as Union Jack bunting fluttered in the sea breeze. An Anglican priest delivered a short prayer. There was a Spitfire flyover. If you ignored all the iPhones and mobility scooters, it was a scene that would have fit in comfortably 80 years ago.

    Sources indicate that by setting out alone on a three-day walk, I was seeking solitude, and moments like that clifftop break, when I had the view all to myself, delivered. But the long way out of the Weymouth hubbub also clarified why walking England’s coastal paths is so approachable—especially for those of us who love the outdoors but want to sleep indoors. Since the country is quite densely populated, you can easily walk the trails from town to town, and hotel to hotel, without the weight (and stress) of camping equipment. For those same reasons, it’s also perfect as a solo walker; the risks feel more manageable when you know medical care is within reach; that you’re rarely without phone service; and that your hotel door locks at night.

    After 12 miles or so of walking, I arrived at West Lulworth, a town of centuries-old stone cottages that can best be described as “quaint.” I was greeted by the famous Durdle Door, a limestone arch that snakes out of a cliff and into the Channel, with clusters of beachgoers splashing underneath. It's a place worth lingering: After going down my final descent of the day, I snuck a peek at Lulworth Cove, a popular bay almost fully enclosed by limestone (and a UNESCO World Heritage Site), before checking into the Old Barn Inn, a B&B up the road for a gloriously hot shower.

    A view of Durdle Door, a limestone arch that can be seen from the trail.

    My second day of walking presented a new challenge: Part of my planned route was closed because it crossed a firing range in use by the Army for training. To avoid it, I rode the bus (the Jurassic Coast is very well served by public transit, at least in summer) part of the way to my next destination, then planned to take a shortcut through some fields to get back to the coast. Sarah, the owner of the Old Barn, had given me extremely specific verbal directions based on local landmarks, which were easy enough to follow until I’d reached the “horrible hill” she warned me of. It was then that I realized I was in the middle of a field with no obvious path out. I bushwhacked to a nearby road, the peace of solitude nowhere to be found as I muttered, “I’ve done this to myself.”.

    It has been revealed that but thanks to my two puny bars of cell phone service, I navigated over another field, through a herd of sheep, along a ravine, and then emerged, alarmingly sweaty, into the absolutely charming limestone village of Worth Matravers. I made a beeline to the local pub (as recommended by Sarah), and enjoyed what was undoubtedly the best pint of my life looking out over a grassy field—and to the ocean beyond. As I sipped my lager at a picnic table, a forceful summer wind whipped off the water, knocking down the pub’s sandwich board advertising Cornish pasties, but it didn’t bother me or the handful of other pubgoers sitting out in the sun.

    Perhaps there is something to the old saying about victory being sweetest after you’ve known defeat, because for all of the frustration I endured that day, the second half of my walk was absolutely breathtaking. After an easy, peaceful meander back down to the coastal path, I spent the next two hours walking through clifftop fields where I saw more deer and cows than humans, and past the famous Danding Ledge, a stone shelf jutting into a patch of sea popular with wild swimming enthusiasts. The wind that had teased me earlier died down closer to the water, and all I could hear was the crash of the waves against the rocks below. When I’ve needed a moment of peace in the few months since then, I’ve summoned the memory of that afternoon and the calm those clifftop fields offered.

    A solo walker making their way along the South West Coast Path.

    I woke up the following morning in the seaside town of Swanage with calves so sore that the thought of any incline made me nervous. To my dismay, I discovered right away that, to pick up the coastal path from the inn where I’d stayed (Rivendell Guest House), I first had to climb a steep staircase from the sandy beach, up the cliff to the bluff. Thankfully, shortly thereafter things flattened out. It was also the busiest section of the trail I encountered—though, even here, I saw only a dozen or so people, mostly locals in athletic gear out for a morning ramble.

    In a recent development, when I reached the hilltop, I was greeted by a few hundred cows—and just beyond their enclosure, the Old Harry Rocks came into view. Millions of years’ worth of waves have chiseled away at this promontory, carving a series of chalk stacks that now sit away from the mainland. I watched two ambitious kayakers appear on the side of the rocks where the water was calmer and stare up at the feat of nature—enjoying a perspective that I’m sure is heavily advised against, and which only few have gotten to enjoy.

    The final part of my walk was along Studland Beach, a sandy four-mile stretch that backs up onto a nature preserve. I waded into the water, sat in the sun, and saw a boat selling ice cream delight children up and down the crowded beach, before reaching the last mile—which also happens to be home to the UK’s most popular naturist (or nudist) beach. The ice cream boat pulled up again, and it tickled me to see that the evenly tanned sexagenarians were just as pleased to have a midday treat as the energetic children I'd just passed.

    Boats bob in the water near Old Harry Rocks in Studland, Dorset.

    The final adventure of my trip also brought out childish delight in me: To get to Bournemouth, where I’d catch a train back to London, I had to take a four-minute ferry ride. Alongside me on the ferry was a double-decker bus with its upper deck open to the elements, letting passengers take full advantage of the beach breeze. The sheer logistics of this was a thrill to witness: a convertible bus driving onto a boat.

    According to recent reports, on the other side of the strait, I got onto that very bus—aptly called The Breezer—and watched as the natural coastline was slowly enveloped by an urban milieu. It was a slightly rude awakening to reemerge into Bournemouth, a small university city where the asphalt had soaked up the sun, presaging the upcoming heatwave. But I realized as I walked through the train station that I was inadvertently grinning with pride. I assumed no one would ask me, a stinky and visibly sweaty woman, what I’d been up to, but if they had, I would have been all too happy to tell them about my solo walk along the South West Coast Path.

    My First “Upcoming” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

    📅 01 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Godsavethepoints

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, there’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card.
    • According to recent reports, the changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards.
    • Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, there’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the fresh changes.

    According to recent reports, the changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

    But what about the redemption of points?

    Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

    Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

    Sources indicate that which leads me to the notable bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a latest “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

    This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

    Industry observers note that previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

    In a recent development, I am in Fresh York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

    In a recent development, typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

    If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

    In a recent development, BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive….

    Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

    A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

    For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

    Recent findings suggest that if Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

    Industry observers note that you can check out the newly introduced 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

    Sources indicate that gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott.

    #31217. Over Arepas and Cachitos, Venezuelans in Madrid Find a Sense of Home

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1518 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Over Arepas and Cachitos, Venezuelans in Madrid Find a Sense of Home

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high.
    • According to recent reports, I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina.
    • The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez says.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high. A digital billboard flashes congratulations for the recent Venezuelan team’s World Baseball Classic win. Nearby, a vendor hawks yellow, blue, and red flags, while signs advertising remittance services to Latin America clutter my sightline. All around me, the Madrid market fills with the round, sing-song accent of Venezuelan Spanish.

    According to recent reports, I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina. The familiar warmth of Latin America—I lived in Mexico before moving to Spain—tears open a pang of nostalgia in my chest. Guests seated at the stainless-steel bar munch on empanadas de carne mechada, continuously reaching for the green, herby salsa guasacaca. “How can it be that they are pumping a million barrels of oil out a day but they cannot fix a single hospital in Caracas?” I overhear another diner say to a friend, discussing the latest spate of frustrations back home.

    The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez says.

    According to recent reports, among Madrid’s 130,000-strong Venezuelan diaspora, these conversations are not uncommon. Spain’s Venezuelan population has swollen to almost 700,000 people, making it the largest community outside of the Americas, and a significant portion of the country’s nearly eight million citizens living abroad. Many have fled their homeland amid the economic and political instability that followed Hugo Chavez’s Bolivarian Revolution and continued under Nicolás Maduro’s rule. Ongoing uncertainty continues to drive migration. Unlike other diasporas, Madrid’s Venezuelan population isn’t concentrated in a single neighborhood. Instead, it stretches across the city and spans a broad socioeconomic spectrum, from delivery drivers and financiers to political exiles.

    Its food institutions mirror a similar range.

    Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez can pinpoint the moment they decided to open a Venezuelan restaurant in Madrid. The two, who moved to Spain in 1997 after a lifetime in the coastal city of Puerto de La Cruz, had gone to meet friends for Venezuelan empanadas at one of the few spots in town at the time. After waiting 45 minutes for their order in a long line of people hankering for a taste of home, Pérez—a natural entrepreneur—saw opportunity.

    Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago.

    Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—is served alongside cachapas, arepas, fried fish, and more.

    When they opened El Empanadazo nearly a decade ago, the couple joined the ranks of just a handful of other Venezuelan food joints. They chose to set up shop in the Mercado de Las Maravillas. “It was really where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” Pérez says of the market. In no time, they were serving hearty plates of Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—crispy fried whole fish, sweet corn griddled cachapas, arepas, and more.

    Recent findings suggest that “Our restaurant really became a gathering place for Venezuelans. I remember the early days when I was spending more time there, seeing people with tears in their eyes,” Pérez notes. “When you’re an immigrant, little things like the taste of home really get to you.”.

    Maira María Gómez and her husband Manuel Pérez Álvarez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago, there were far fewer Venezuelan restaurants in the city.

    At the time, Venezuelan food wasn’t as easy to find and people went out of their way for it. Today, a quick search for “arepa” on the delivery apps will turn up hundreds of options. “Now there are lots of spots, but we were really pioneers, and it wasn’t even all that long ago,” Pérez claims.

    It has been revealed that be it Arepa’s Coffee Shop nestled next to the hustle of the Moncloa train and bus station, or the four-location La Arepera, the Insta-famous El Chino Venezolano, or the fast-growing Guasacaca, the country’s gastronomic footprint continues to grow alongside its diaspora in Madrid. At the March 2026 Arepa Fest, a celebration of Venezuelan and Colombian food and culture, in the north edges of Madrid, more than 5,000 people gathered to snack on the region's signature split- and stuffed-cornmeal snack, while the sound system alternated between pumping Venezuelan Merengue and reggaeton.

    At Panadería Torrerí, warm pastries like cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, keep customers coming back.

    In a recent development, A similar fervor can be felt at Panadería Torrerí. By mid-morning, the team is already replenishing their glass case of cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, and brushed with panela (unrefined cane sugar) and anise. Regulars grab a table and owner Mara Azuaje, always poised with a “¿Cómo está usted?” promptly ferries over their order.

    Azuaje opened her bakery in 2024 to bring traditional Venezuelan pastries to the neighborhood of Barrio de Salamanca. For years, there had been no Venezuelan bakery in the area, despite this upscale neighborhood being nicknamed “Little Caracas” for its substantial diaspora. Today, Panadería Torrerí attracts both affluent property owners alongside motorbike messengers, all looking for a taste of home.

    Mara Azuaje opened Panadería Torrerí in the Barrio de Salamanca in 2024.

    It has been revealed that azuaje, who came to Spain at 27, knows what they're after. She spent years working odd jobs to save the money needed to open her bakery. “I cleaned homes, worked as a delivery driver, took care of children. I did whatever, but I was always very ambitious,” Azuaje says. “I wanted to have my own business.”.

    Industry observers note that she didn’t understand the exact shape it would take, but her grandmother’s lessons to her as a child around the importance of learning an oficio, a craft, stayed with her. “I was always baking with my grandmother who told me I needed to know how to do something, so I opened a bakery,” she claims. Today, Azuaje is proud to be known across the neighborhood for her homemade bread and her hearty rolled-dough pastries.

    Sources indicate that other Venezuelan restaurant owners transitioned into hospitality later in life. At Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa’s Cafetín, the menu—arepas with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado for breakfast, or creamed curry soup and sweet corn and hearty salads for lunch—carries traces of Venezuela while honoring the other places the couple has called home.

    At Cafetín, the menu showcases Venezuelan flavors through a global lens.

    Cafetín's arepas are stuffed with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado.

    According to recent reports, the married pair came to Madrid after a full life in Caracas. “By 2007 Chávez just kept winning and winning, and things were getting worse and worse. It really scared us,” Felipe claims. That year was Chávez’s first attempt at constitutional reform to remove presidential term limits and expand state control of the economy. He lost his bid but remained in power and went on to secure reform in 2009. So, when the bank Fossa worked for offered him a job in Zurich, they didn’t hesitate. It was a decision that has led to many years of living abroad.

    Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa say that their Cafetín has become a hub for Venezuelans, who connect over coffee and arepas.

    Their clientele reflects a similar worldliness, with Venezuelans who arrived directly from Caracas but also those who have made it here by way of a university in Boston, or lived for years in Miami, New York, or London. Cafetín is a meeting point where these Venezuelans intersect, creating a community within a community. As Castelló Castro put it, “empiezas a hacer nexo”—you start to make connections.

    It has been revealed that recently, I'm told, a couple in a sunlit corner of the cafe started chatting with a man standing at the long bar after hearing him mention Caracas. They began tracing the routes through Miami and Upcoming York that had brought them to Madrid. Another day, a college sweatshirt prompted a conversation—and a new friendship. “It’s beautiful to see, especially in difficult moments in Venezuela,” says Castelló Castro.

    Back at the Mercado de Las Maravillas, I sit at Buda Bar watching the lunch rush fade, as owner Rebeksa Mouzaber prepares me a sweet-corn crescent-shaped cachapa, its edges lacy from a bed of hot butter on the flattop griddle. A food courier accepts a freshly-made pocket-sized empanada while he scrolls and waits for his order.

    Venezuelans like coming here because they feel at home—not just in the dishes that are served but also in the way they are asked for, Mouzaber tells me. “We know what it means when they ask for an ñapa (a top-up), just like we know how it feels to be so far away from home.”.

    #31216. Delta Air Lines CEO Called Wi-Fi Essential, Now Says Passengers Don’t Choose Airlines For It

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1240 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Delta Air Lines CEO Called Wi-Fi Essential, Now Says Passengers Don’t Choose Airlines For It

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian once called connectivity essential to daily life and promised an onboard experience resembling what passengers enjoy on the ground.
    • Speaking with Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum on November 16, Bastian defended Delta’s connectivity strategy.
    • “This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian once called connectivity essential to daily life and promised an onboard experience resembling what passengers enjoy on the ground. Now, defending the decision to wait for Amazon Leo rather than install Starlink, he says customers do not choose airlines based on Wi-Fi. I understand the argument he is trying to make, but Delta spent years teaching passengers to expect more from their internet connection. Some of us listened.

    Speaking with Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum on November 16, Bastian defended Delta’s connectivity strategy.

    “This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”.

    In a recent development, he acknowledged enjoying Starlink himself, explained that Delta and SpaceX could not agree on a business model, and expressed confidence that Amazon could deliver a competitive alternative. Bastian also defended the existing Viasat product, describing it as “pretty darn close” to Starlink.

    We can debate his last point, but his broader claim about how customers choose airlines strikes me as far too dismissive, especially considering what he has noted before.

    According to recent reports, when Delta announced its free Wi-Fi initiative in January 2023, Bastian described connectivity in very different terms. Back then, he noted:.

    “At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different.”.

    In the accompanying T-Mobile announcement, he added:.

    “The ability to stay connected while seeing the world is simply foundational.”.

    Sources indicate that I agreed with him. Delta made fast, free Wi-Fi part of its premium proposition. The message was that passengers could expect a more useful and enjoyable flight because they could remain connected.

    In a recent development, the airline has continued making that case. Its own explanation of why travelers should choose Delta includes fast, free Wi-Fi among the benefits it promotes.

    Now that its primary competitor, United, is rapidly approaching a point in which it will have a superior internet product, the message sounds more like passengers should focus on everything else.

    I tend to give people the benefit of the doubt and Bastian is no exception.

    Sources indicate that saying connectivity is essential does not necessarily mean passengers will select the airline with the fastest connection. Bastian could reasonably argue that Delta already provides sufficiently good Wi-Fi and that another improvement in speed will not overcome differences in schedules, service, or loyalty.

    But saying customers do not choose airlines based on Wi-Fi goes considerably further. Some certainly do. I am one of them. Delta cannot spend years promoting connectivity as part of what makes its product worth choosing, then expect no scrutiny when its CEO downplays connectivity as a reason to choose a competitor.

    Perhaps Bastian has data showing that relatively few passengers have changed their booking habits. I would be interested in seeing it. His statement, however, leaves little room for customers whose behavior already contradicts it. He’s essentially inviting them to fly to United instead.

    Not that I fly Delta often, but unlike some of my colleagues I’ve had very good experiences with Wi-Fi on Delta.

    The Viasat Wi-Fi I have used on both American Airlines and Delta has generally been fine for the work I do. I can work on the blog, handle email, and complete other tasks without needing the fastest connection available.

    It has been revealed that starlink or Viasat, I just need my connection to work and I should not have to wonder whether it will (one reason there are many aircraft on United, like the 757-300, that I avoid like the plague). If Viasat lets me accomplish what I need to accomplish, that flight remains productive and I’m a happy passenger. I am not going to pretend otherwise simply because I prefer Starlink.

    But Starlink has raised my expectations. It is objectively faster and more responsive and it more closely resembles working from the ground…always. When I have comparable options, that influences my decision. I have already explained how I try to improve my odds of finding Starlink on United Airlines.

    Recent findings suggest that that does not mean I would accept any fare or routing to get it, but it means connectivity enters the calculation alongside departure time and price, particularly on a daytime flight. For someone whose work travels with him, several productive hours onboard have immense value…and I cannot relax on a plane if there is work to be done (that miserable United 777 flight from SFO-EWR comes to mind).

    Bastian is right that passengers evaluate the total experience, but the internet connection is part of that experience and increasingly a critical part of the experience as passengers expectations evolve.

    A good crew and comfortable seat are welcome and in some ways foundational, but so is being able to finish work before landing rather than spending the evening catching up instead of spending it with my family.

    Sources indicate that different passengers will assign different values to those things. Someone taking a vacation may be delighted to disconnect. Someone traveling during the workday may be far more concerned about whether the connection will support the tasks waiting on a laptop. I do not expect Bastian to concede that every passenger should leave Delta for United, which is just a stupid argument. But recognizing that connectivity can influence a booking would hardly undermine the rest of Delta’s product…Bastian suddenly sounds defensive and tone deaf.

    It would simply acknowledge how some customers use their time onboard….

    I have defended the commercial logic behind Delta choosing Amazon Leo. An airline has legitimate reasons to consider control over its passenger interface and the broader business relationship when selecting a technology partner. We should also welcome competition for Starlink. Having another capable provider would be good for airlines and passengers.

    It has been revealed that but Delta intends to begin installing Leo on an initial 500 aircraft in 2028. That leaves time for competitors to establish upcoming expectations, even if Amazon ultimately delivers an excellent product. As I discussed earlier this week, the failed launch carrying 40 Amazon satellites illustrates the execution risk involved in waiting for a network still being built, even if Delta has multiple back-up options.

    It has been revealed that delta may have made the right long-term choice: only time will tell. But that does not mean passengers will ignore what competitors offer in the meantime and I’m fairly comfortable in saying Delta will lose a fair number of customers due to its Wi-Fi disparity with United.

    It has been revealed that bastian once described connectivity as essential and foundational. He was right then, making his recent remarks puzzling, even when taken in context. I also concede that the Viasat service on American and Delta has generally worked well for my needs. This is not a case of Starlink being the only usable internet in the sky.

    But reliable Wi-Fi now influences which flights I book, and Starlink increasingly gives me another reason to choose one departure over another and specifically, to choose United Airlines over others. Delta helped make connectivity something passengers expect. It should not be surprised when passengers begin choosing airlines based on who delivers it best.

    #31214. Industry News: Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1004 w)

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s upcoming ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s upcoming ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., remarked, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five newly introduced air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    According to recent reports, they justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, mentioned Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz noted the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization initiative so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    In a recent development, senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., noted after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    Sources indicate that for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., remarked the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    It has been revealed that “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he noted. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy stated, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create complications in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    According to recent reports, the telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford stated Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    Bedford noted he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    It has been revealed that “I was on tour in June and July for my newly introduced stand-up hour and managed to escape the crazy heat wave in Europe when I performed in Reykjavík, Iceland. It was my first time there, so it was quite exotic to experience the cold in July. (I live in LA, where it feels like it's getting hotter every summer.) There is a crispness that is so unique. I was with my family—my kids and my baby daddy—and Sheng Wang, who was opening all my shows. The landscape is so breathtaking. Just driving by geysers bursting and steaming out of the ground felt like witnessing magic. Whenever I travel my favorite thing is going to the biggest supermarket and buying any local snacks you can't get anywhere else. Our tour guide, Aron Karlsson, had taken us to the Bónus grocery store, where we got a ton of fish jerky and black licorice with marzipan, and we were snacking on them on our way to the Blue Lagoon while listening to Björk's jazz album, Gling-Gló. (A very fun part of being in Iceland is passing by every stranger and asking yourself, Is that Björk? Is that Björk? Please be Björk.) Then we got there and went straight into this opaque, milky-blue water; it was kind of like being in a luxurious version of that cloudy bath in Minority Report that [Samantha Morton] lies in. There was a mask bar in the lagoon, where you can apply a silica mud mask, an algae mask, or a mineral mask to your face, and it all felt very thick, goopy, and smooth on the skin. We're Asian and all have eczema, so we experienced a lot of relief afterward. It was very cute seeing families with members of all ages, including my children, wading around the lagoon together with spa masks on their face. Then Sheng—and this is very Sheng—started harvesting the silica off the walls and putting it on his face. Since it was free, we all copied him. I'm not sure if that was good for us or not.”.

    • Waiting more than two hours for your checked bag is frustrating.
    • Passengers aboard American Airlines flight 2609 from Miami (MIA) to Atlanta (ATL) on November 16, 2026, reported an unpleasant surprise at baggage claim.
    • Passenger Derick McCallum recorded the scene and later questioned the airline’s explanation:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Waiting more than two hours for your checked bag is frustrating. Watching it emerge covered in a brown substance that looks like human waste is considerably worse. That is what American Airlines passengers reported in Atlanta this week, though the airline claims the mess had a much less revolting explanation: peanut butter.

    Passengers aboard American Airlines flight 2609 from Miami (MIA) to Atlanta (ATL) on November 16, 2026, reported an unpleasant surprise at baggage claim. Travelers waited more than two hours before their luggage appeared on carousel eight at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. When the bags arrived, passengers saw a brown substance smeared across them and naturally feared the worst.

    Passenger Derick McCallum recorded the scene and later questioned the airline’s explanation:.

    “Even if somebody did pack peanut butter? How much peanut butter does somebody pack to cover that many bags?”.

    (my mind goes to Diddy Combs and AstroGlide…).

    In a recent development, american later said that liquefied peanut butter had leaked from a passenger’s checked bag, affecting nearby luggage. The airline said an environmental inspection confirmed its explanation.

    “Unfortunately, a food item from a customer’s checked bag leaked during the flight, affecting several bags nearby.”.

    I would certainly prefer peanut butter to the alternative passengers feared. But I would still be rather unhappy about finding someone else’s sandwich spread having spoiled my suitcase.

    It isn’t clear how much peanut butter was involved, how it was packaged, or exactly how it spread…feel free to speculate.

    According to recent reports, passengers complained they were left cleaning their luggage with disinfecting wipes and tissues. American apologized and remarked it would work directly with affected customers to resolve the situation. Since the baggage was delayed two hours anyway, did the stuff look even worse before? Or did a baggage handler throw the peanut butter bag and thereby cause the apparent explosion in the first place?

    I check bags when necessary, particularly when traveling with my family. But stories like this reinforce why I prefer to keep my belongings with me when possible. Even if you carefully pack your own suitcase, you have no control over what someone else puts in theirs. While that’s true in a shared overhead bin too, it’s much less likely to be a problem.

    There is some dark humor in a baggage carousel full of passengers trying to determine whether what that brown stuff was all over their bag, but I’m sure there was nothing to laugh about if that was your bag covered in brown.

    Sources indicate that american Airlines claims peanut butter leaking from a checked bag caused the brown mess passengers discovered on their luggage in Atlanta. Better than the alternative, I suppose, but I hope American follows through promptly on cleaning or otherwise resolving the damage for affected passengers. Yuck!

    Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1420 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that senate Minority Leader Charles E.
    • It has been revealed that senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
    • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    It has been revealed that senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting remarked the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    Sources indicate that “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    It has been revealed that “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    Sources indicate that sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    Sources indicate that sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, stated, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she remarked.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday noted at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    Industry observers note that “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he remarked. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the newly introduced ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    According to recent reports, several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve remarked many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who noted he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he noted. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he remarked. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    In a recent development, senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    Sources indicate that “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan stated.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    Recent findings suggest that “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he noted. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    It has been revealed that sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    • American Airlines prepares to refresh and expand its three Admirals Club lounges at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.
    • The carrier said Tuesday that it will add seating, upgrade amenities, and improve food and beverage service across all three spaces in Terminal 4.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines prepares to refresh and expand its three Admirals Club lounges at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.

    The carrier said Tuesday that it will add seating, upgrade amenities, and improve food and beverage service across all three spaces in Terminal 4.

    In the near term, the Admirals Club lounge in Concourse A between gates A19 and A21 will get a new servery area, infrastructure enhancements to support expanded food and beverage offerings, and facility updates to improve the overall customer experience.

    In a recent development, longer-term plans call for nearly tripling the combined footprint of the Concourse A lounges, the other being above gates A7-A9. New furniture and finishings will be brought in, and seating capacity will expand by 150%.

    The lounge in Concourse B, between gates B5 and B7, will get a fresh self-service food and beverage area and have its seating capacity increased by 20%.

    Sources indicate that “Phoenix continues to be an important hub in our network, and these investments reflect our commitment to giving customers more space, comfort, and convenience when they travel through PHX,” American Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden said in a news release. “While we look forward to the development of the fresh West Terminal, these enhancements will help create an even more seamless travel experience for the millions of customers who pass through Phoenix each year.”.

    The planned West Terminal will be built on the west side of the airport between Terminal 3 and Taxiway U. American is expected to serve as the terminal’s primary carrier.

    According to the airport’s timeline, the project should be finished by 2033.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    My trip to Latest York on Air France began with a short domestic flight on the Embraer 170 in business class from Basel to Paris, a short and pleasant journey.

    Years ago after my La Premiere flight from Los Angeles to Paris, I continued on to Basel on an Embraer 190 in what Air France marketed as business class. But the service onboard was no different than economy class: there was no blocked middle seat, meal, or beverages served in glass..it was just regular economy class service.

    But Air France has come a long way and I feel like even on a short domestic business class flight it really has really raised the bar in terms of service.

    I booked my ticket from Basel to New York JFK via Paris for 60,000 Flying Blue miles and $453 in business class, booking just 36 hours prior to departure (so yes, Air France does release last-minute award space).

    Basel Airport straddles Switzerland and France. I entered on the French side and checked in for my flight.

    On the check-in level you can walk back and forth freely between the French and Swiss side, but on the lower level and upper level there’s a physical barrier. For example, I went out to the terrace on the upper level and there’s a fence separating the two nations.

    After visiting the Skyview Lounge, now operated by Aspire, I headed to the gate for boarding at 1:45 pm, which began right on schedule.

    Stepping onboard, I found my seat in 2F.

    Industry observers note that the aircraft has 76 seats in a 2-2 configuration. Each seat has 31 inches of pitch and is 18 inches wide. Seats recline three inches. There are individual air vents, but no power of any kind: neither USB or a universal power socket.

    Business class can be adjusted according to demand, the “genius” of having the same seat. On today’s flight there were three rows of business class, but only three passengers: we each had our own row. Air France now blocks adjacent seats in business class, so that is a big advantage versus economy class.

    The only other business class distinctive was that each seat had a pillow and water bottle:.

    At only 250 miles, there wasn’t  much time for a meal service.

    In a recent development, air France nevertheless offers business class passengers a small meal box on its shorthaul network, part of a catering concept introduced in 2024 and developed with Servair Corporate Chef François Adamski, a Bocuse d’Or winner and Meilleur Ouvrier de France. For flights departing after 10:00 am, Air France serves what it calls a “signature” sandwich along with a French sweet or dessert, with the selection changing regularly. It is served in a sturdy cardboard box.

    On my flight, the meal consisted of two finger sandwiches with smoked salmon and a creamy herb filling on brown bread, along with a small pecan tart and a chocolate…a very nice treat. The airline also serves wine and Champagne in proper glassware, though I just had sparkling water on this flight.

    > Read More: Air France Served This Surprisingly Elegant Business Class Meal On A 250-Mile Flight.

    Flight attendants onboard were very polite and efficient: meals and drinks were offered immediately and refills offered after they had completed service in economy class and again before landing, all on a very short flight.

    This flight has no internet and no in-flight-entertainment, but Starlink is coming to these jets.

    However, it was a beautiful day tempearture wise and I enjoyed looking out the window, especially as we flew over Paris (thought it was a bit hazy) as we neared CDG.

    In a recent development, business class passengers have a dedicated lavatory in the font of the cabin. It was small but clean.

    We landed on time in Paris where I ran into a fairly complicated connection to Terminal 2E Hall M…but it was a short but lovely flight.

    Türkiye Just Confirmed a Latest Golden Visa Starting at $150,000
