    #31181. Can Rocky Save the World?

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (791 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    Can Rocky Save the World?

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sylvester Stallone has been a Hollywood institution for so long — his breakthrough movie Rocky premiered 50 years ago — that his previous underdog status as a struggling actor seems perfectly mythic in the upcoming behind-the-scenes biographical drama I Play Rocky.
    • Industry observers note that the fairy-tale aspect of I Play Rocky comes from its background story.
    • Recent findings suggest that starting with Stallone practicing elocution (using Walt Whitman’s “I Sing the Body Electric”) to soften his rough Latest York accent, the film then places him against odds in an era of cultural ferment that included such films as Altman’s The Long Goodbye and Coppola’s The Conversation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sylvester Stallone has been a Hollywood institution for so long — his breakthrough movie Rocky premiered 50 years ago — that his previous underdog status as a struggling actor seems perfectly mythic in the upcoming behind-the-scenes biographical drama I Play Rocky.

    Industry observers note that the fairy-tale aspect of I Play Rocky comes from its background story. In this, young Stallone (played by Anthony Ippolito) is a virtually homeless outsider, working at a movie theater, who after spending 16 months on writing eight screenplays, joins the creative zeitgeist of 1970s Hollywood, also known as the American Renaissance. It is this personal journey that illuminates the Stallone legend that climaxes with Rocky winning the Academy Award for best picture over such esteemed movies as Taxi Driver, Network, Bound for Glory, and All the President’s Men.

    Recent findings suggest that starting with Stallone practicing elocution (using Walt Whitman’s “I Sing the Body Electric”) to soften his rough Latest York accent, the film then places him against odds in an era of cultural ferment that included such films as Altman’s The Long Goodbye and Coppola’s The Conversation. (Stallone pays particular attention to the intonation of Coppola’s actors repeating the line “He’d kill us if he found out.”) Screenwriter Peter Gamble doesn’t make that detail ominous but simplifies the life-or-death aspect of Stallone’s career and artistic ambition as part of the wannabe actor’s desperate, working-class consciousness — inspired by viewing the heavyweight championship boxing match between Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner. It’s easier to take than the sociological theme in Green Book, the egregious previous film of director Peter Farrelly. I Play Rocky regains the genial humanism of such Farrelly brothers’ movies as Me, Myself and Irene, Stuck on You, and The Ringer, and especially the Farrelly brothers’ script for Outside Providence.

    Kiki Seto (Talia Shire) and Anthony Ippolito (Sylvester Stallone) in I Play Rocky.

    Stallone’s ambition is epitomized by his insistence that the Rocky screenplay he wrote in four days and sold to producers Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff can be filmed only starring himself. He demands, “I play Rocky.” That’s not a playground taunt in the milieu of financial bargaining and egotism that’s gleefully depicted by a series of Hollywood types — P. J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell as Winkler and Chartoff, Rob Demery as Joe Frazier, and a standout cameo by Trevor St. John as a self-serious fight coordinator.

    Recent findings suggest that in Hollywood’s gladiatorial circus, Stallone’s striving and eventual success become a credible moral victory. He must claim his own identity and career path separately from his worldly father Frank (Matt Dillon gives a moving characterization of a parent’s cynicism, affection, and personal regret). His wife Sasha (AnnaSophie Robb) encourages him: “I’d rather be optimistic and be wrong than pessimistic and be right.” These backstage details (including a hostile producer who dismisses Stallone as “a droopy-eyed hack actor”) make I Play Rocky a credible and appealing saga of Stallone’s indefatigable confidence. The movie rejects the sort of dark, objectionable narcissism that we saw in the Springsteen hagiography Deliver Me from Nowhere.

    It is important that the filmmakers accurately measure Rocky’s significance. Farrelly and Gamble mix film history with good sense and humor when portraying wild-eyed director John Avildsen (Jay Duplass) deep in his own world of pragmatic professionalism (“Great art never comes through compromise”). They also capture Stallone’s own, uncanny sense of achieving the proper effect — not so much when Rocky emotes to his manager Mickey as when, in a startling shot, he points to details in a massive-screen image of Kirk Douglas in Champion, from 1948.

    Sources indicate that putting Rocky in proper perspective is a curatorial feat. It recognizes Stallone’s film as a work of pop lore. Its popularity gave Hollywood the opportunity to ignore scary powerful art like Scorsese’s Taxi Driver in favor of the folk and commercial elements that are easily enjoyed in American culture — although missing from Millennial film culture. Remember: In 1976, Rocky seemed an artificial retread of old boxing films, pilfering the ethnic sentimentality of Marty, On the Waterfront, and Requiem for a Heavyweight as if Muhammad Ali had never happened.

    According to recent reports, but I Play Rocky works differently. It recalls Stallone’s response to Wepner (“This guy won’t go down!”) to achieve the authentic Millennial pop lore of Better Man, Song Sung Blue, Back 2 America, Power Ballad, and the upcoming Madden. (These restorative myths correct the disappointing Creed sequels that failed to live up to Rocky.) I Play Rocky channels Stallone’s personal perseverance to enlighten our current demoralized sensibilities.

    Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of Upcoming Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

    Latest Update: Flexibility: How Flight Attendants Can Be Displaced From Their Schedule With Little Notice

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, flight attendants' schedules in the US can change at short notice in several ways, but union contracts set limits on how it happens and what they're paid when it does.
    • According to recent reports, in the rest of the world, it's a little bit different, and unions rarely have much input.
    • When a trip or part of a trip is canceled, crew scheduling can move the affected flight attendant to another trip, put them on reserve/standby, or release them from duty entirely.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, flight attendants' schedules in the US can change at short notice in several ways, but union contracts set limits on how it happens and what they're paid when it does. This guide will take a closer look at how it all works, when things change at the last minute, and what can happen to a flight attendant's schedule.

    According to recent reports, in the rest of the world, it's a little bit different, and unions rarely have much input. It's all down to the airlines' operations teams and aviation regulators when it comes to how our schedules can change. Of course, flexibility is key, and things can happen unexpectedly, but that's all part of the fun of being a flight attendant or cabin crew.

    When a trip or part of a trip is canceled, crew scheduling can move the affected flight attendant to another trip, put them on reserve/standby, or release them from duty entirely. One older contract, filed with the SEC, pays them for whichever is greater: the original assignment or the new one. Many US airline contracts call this "pay protection." This is a contractual rule that keeps a flight attendant's scheduled pay credit safe when flights change, get canceled, or get delayed through no fault of their own.

    If the trip or a leg of the sequence is canceled, union collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) typically guarantee that they still get paid for the original scheduled value or the new assigned trip, whichever is greater. If crew scheduling alters the route or equipment after a disruption, pay protection ensures that they do not lose money if the new assignment ends up paying less than what was originally on the line.

    In a recent development, alaska Airlines' current agreement, for example, can remove a flight attendant from an assignment with pay protection and fly them home as a passenger; this is called deadheading. Under the 2025-2028 Collective Bargaining Agreement between Alaska Airlines and the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, line-holding flight attendants receive 150% pay on top of strong base trip protection when crew scheduling reassigns or reroutes a sequence. If a crew member is assigned to four or more legs over the original sequence, pay is 200%.

    Sources indicate that trip displacement occurs when a crew member is involuntarily removed from a scheduled flight pairing or stranded away from their planned itinerary. This could be due to operational needs, regulatory limits, or personnel bumps; it is not a personal absence from duty. It can vary from airline to airline in the US, and union contracts may vary. At carriers without union contracts, such as Delta Air Lines, displaced flight attendants often do not receive automatic pay protection and must choose between sitting on-call availability or taking a lesser payment.

    Recent findings suggest that A flight attendant can also be bumped from a trip that they bid for. They can be displaced from trips to make room for training or for upcoming hires' supervised flights, which are called operating experience. A flight attendant can be pulled from a trip so a supervisor, for example, can occupy that position for qualification or observation. In those cases, the displaced flight attendant gets a similar trip or is released from duty for the rest of the trip.

    According to recent reports, frontier Airlines' 2019 contract requires at least 24 hours' notice before a flight attendant is displaced, and pays them for the trip they lost. Depending on the contract, crew scheduling may have a specific window (often matching the original trip's footprint) to assign replacement flights. If the airline does not reassign the flight attendant within those rules, the crew member is released with pay.

    Sources indicate that the one thing that most often catches US flight attendants off guard is the junior assignment, sometimes called junior availability or JA. This is a last-resort scheduling measure where an airline forces the most junior legal flight attendant to work a flight during their scheduled day off or open time because all reserve crews have been exhausted. This prevents cancellations or other disruptions when the reserve pool runs out, and it typically falls on the most junior available flight attendant.

    Recent findings suggest that this is used in cases such as major weather disruptions, holiday travel spikes, or high sick-call volume, after all on-call reserve flight attendants have already been assigned. Airlines assign these open trips starting from the absolute bottom of the seniority list at that base and working upward until the flight is covered. However, the new trip cannot violate mandatory rest requirements or maximum duty limits. This will also attract a premium payment, and the airline has to restore any lost days off.

    Recent findings suggest that contracts usually limit how often junior assignments can happen. PSA Airlines' contract caps it at three days a month and bars assignments that are more than 24 hours in advance, while Silver Airways' contract limits it to twice a month. They also usually pay at a premium rate of 150% at Silver Airways and PSA Airlines, and 2.5 times the trip rate under Alaska Airlines' 2025–2028 contract. Silver Airways closed down in June 2025.

    It has been revealed that at some airlines, flight attendants who are already on duty at the airport, such as those arriving, checking in, or waiting in between flights, can be drafted onto another flight when time is critical, or the reserve pool is empty. Therefore, their entire schedule can change if a fresh trip is added or removed. Usually, crew scheduling tries not to disrupt the schedule too much and swaps them with a trip with similar timing, but of course, this is not always possible.

    Flight attendants on reserve or standby are usually more junior crew with low seniority, are on call, and can be given trips with little notice. Many US-based crew start out on reserve and may do so for the first few years. At American Airlines, for example, flight attendants are on reserve for the first year and then move to one month on reserve, one month off reserve until year five, when it moves to one month on reserve and three months off according to their APFA contract.

    At Delta Air Lines, junior flight attendants bid on a line and do not have to complete a full month on reserve. Instead, they have six 'A' days a month, where they are on call. If a Delta flight attendant's trip is canceled or removed, they only keep their pay if they convert to availability. Delta's order of assignment places displaced lineholders on availability ahead of A-Day reserves, and management holds broader discretion to modify trips during irregular operations.

    Airlines in the rest of the world rarely have union agreements, and schedules are set by the operations or crew scheduling department. Rosters are scheduled four to six weeks in advance in accordance with duty time regulations, so you know what your trips will be and your days off, if all goes to strategy. Long-haul rosters don't change much, but short-haul rosters are more likely to change. There is no bidding for trips, although crew can sometimes request one or two trips a month; it is rare that they are given. Part-time work is very rare.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition, every crew member has some standby days, usually three or four per month, when you are on call to cover a trip at short notice because a flight attendant calls in sick or misses a trip. These are periods of around six to eight hours, and you would hope to be called at the beginning, not the end, of the shift. This can be at base, at the airport, or home standby; it varies by airline. Standby isn't just given to junior cabin crew; everyone has to do it, although seniority remains key throughout your career.

    Some airlines also have available days that are filled 12 to 24 hours in advance; you could get a trip, standby duty, or be stood down, and then it becomes a day off. If a change is made to your schedule by operations, it demonstrates up on your roster, and that's it; you do the trip. There is no payment protection pay, sit pay, or any extra payments for schedule changes. Rosters are more likely to change at the last minute due to being called out on standby duty or if a flight is delayed and doesn't allow enough rest, but it is more likely on a short-haul or mixed-fleet roster.

    Every contract is different, so the rules, limits, and premium pay vary widely by airline and by where you are working. Large international airlines in Europe and the UK are not heavily unionized like those in the US, and they have no influence on your schedule or what you actually earn; that is up to the airline itself. In the Middle East, there are no unions.

    In a recent development, the contracts noted here are for comparison to show how contracts have changed in recent years and are for reference only; not all the airlines still exist, and some may have merged. American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and Southwest Airlines contracts have all changed significantly in recent years, affecting how flight attendants are scheduled and paid. Delta's flight attendants are not unionized, so their scheduling rules come from company policy rather than a contract.

    Terminology used by airlines can also be different. In the UK, Europe, and the Middle East, instead of reserve, we have standby, and instead of operating experience for junior flight attendants, we have supernumerary flights. We do not have "junior assignment," "junior availability," "drafting," "reassignment," and "displacement," which can all mean slightly different things depending on the contract. Although it's the same job with the same rules, the terminology, scheduling system, and pay are very different.

    Industry News: Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that president Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov.
    • Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of concerns even as he appears politically weakened at home.
    • Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that president Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images).

    Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of concerns even as he appears politically weakened at home.

    Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

    Industry observers note that the U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

    Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, remarked Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one glitch with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

    “As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

    Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”.

    Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., stated part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

    “They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” stated Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

    That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

    Industry observers note that “I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump remarked Monday. “I think he's backing down.”.

    Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a substantial reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

    It has been revealed that senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”.

    Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, remarked he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”.

    It has been revealed that “I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine stated. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”.

    According to recent reports, during remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

    “Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

    Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

    In a recent development, “Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”.

    But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

    He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

    Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, noted Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”.

    Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the firm’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

    The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”.

    Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Challenges at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”.

    It has been revealed that “Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear problems dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    JetBlue is growing its presence in Central America and the Caribbean.

    For the first time ever, the carrier will serve the Honduran capital of Tegucigalpa. Starting Feb. 25, 2027, flights from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, will arrive at Palmerola International Airport in Comayagua, which serves Tegucigalpa.

    Currently, JetBlue’s only destination in Honduras is San Pedro Sula, in the country’s northwest.

    On Feb. 23, the carrier will launch service between Fort Lauderdale and George Town, Grand Cayman, in the Cayman Islands.

    Both routes will operate daily, using a mix of Airbus A320 and A220 aircraft.

    Recent findings suggest that jetBlue will also offer limited-time daily service from Fort Lauderdale to Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, between Jan. 29 and Feb. 15. The connection will help travelers reach the islands during Carnival, the airline mentioned.

    Sources indicate that “We’re grateful for the way customers across South Florida continue to embrace JetBlue, and we’re committed to delivering even more of the destinations and travel options they’re looking for,” Daniel Shurz, JetBlue’s senior vice president of revenue, network, and enterprise planning, said in a news release. “With new international service to Honduras and Grand Cayman, we’re strengthening Fort Lauderdale’s role as a key gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean, making it easier for customers to reconnect with loved ones, explore new places, and travel across our growing network.”.

    American has prioritized Latin America as demand from U.S. markets, especially Miami, grows. The carrier just recently released service to Barranquilla and Cali in Colombia and will add Barcelona, Venezuela, to its network in January.

    Breaking: Private Pilot Disputes Trump’s Claim That He Used Non-US ATC To Fly In US Airspace Before Office

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Trump has revived a claim that his private pilot previously relied on another country's air traffic control (ATC) system while flying in the US, prompting a public rebuttal from a private pilot.
    • The comments came one week after a nationwide FAA ground stop disrupted thousands of flights and just days after the administration requested another $50.1 billion for aviation modernization.
    • Industry observers note that according to the Daily Beast, Trump made the remarks during a "bonkers appearance" at a White House press conference addressing recent disruptions involving aviation, banking and communications networks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Trump has revived a claim that his private pilot previously relied on another country's air traffic control (ATC) system while flying in the US, prompting a public rebuttal from a private pilot. Speaking during a White House press conference on Friday, Trump criticized America's aviation infrastructure while discussing recent disruptions affecting the country's airspace, according to National Public Radio (NPR).

    The comments came one week after a nationwide FAA ground stop disrupted thousands of flights and just days after the administration requested another $50.1 billion for aviation modernization. However, Trump's account of using foreign controllers has raised questions about whether he meant air traffic control or the navigation technology installed aboard his aircraft.

    Industry observers note that according to the Daily Beast, Trump made the remarks during a "bonkers appearance" at a White House press conference addressing recent disruptions involving aviation, banking and communications networks. Asked about the incidents, the president maintained that they were unrelated, before discussing his personal experiences with private aviation.

    Trump described US ATC infrastructure as "ancient", and mentioned that his pilot had used foreign air traffic control before he entered office.

    “It's ancient! In fact, you know, before I was here, I had a plane. I had a very nice life. And my pilot would use the air traffic control from a totally different country. This was years ago, before I was in office. I don't want to say the country, but he found one country better than ours.”.

    The assertion prompted a response from journalist Brian Karem, who identified himself as a private pilot. In a post on X, Karem disputed the suggestion that pilots operating in US airspace could bypass domestic controllers by seeking assistance from another country. His objection centered on the distinction between the authorities controlling airspace and the equipment pilots use to navigate.

    In a recent development, "You cannot call up ATC in Europe and say, 'Hey give me a hand. I'm flying over US airspace.'".

    Trump's remarks were not entirely latest. During the National Prayer Breakfast in February last year, he similarly claimed to use equipment or services from another country when landing his private aircraft in New York, according to Anadolu Ajansı. The comments attracted scrutiny from aviation experts at the time, Forbes reported.

    Industry observers note that president Trump likely confused air traffic control systems with onboard navigation technology, according to Forbes. Retired airline pilot and aviation safety expert John Cox explained that pilots operating under ATC supervision must comply with the applicable rules of that country, regardless of their navigation equipment's country of origin.

    It has been revealed that air traffic control and aircraft navigation perform very different functions. Controllers concern clearances, instructions and traffic information, while onboard navigation systems help pilots determine their position and follow flight plans. An aircraft operating under instrument flight rules in controlled US airspace cannot simply select a foreign ATC provider. The differences are summarized below:.

    Provides clearances, traffic separation and instructions.

    Provides satellite-based positioning and navigation.

    Calculates and manages the aircraft's flight path.

    Inertial reference system (IRS).

    Tracks aircraft position and movement using onboard sensors.

    Provide route, waypoint and procedure information.

    Provide navigation, communication or flight management capabilities.

    Industry observers note that A plausible explanation is that Trump's aircraft used internationally manufactured avionics, navigation databases, or satellite-based positioning technology. As the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Aeronautical Information Manual explains, these technologies provide navigation guidance but do not replace ATC services. Without confirmation from Trump's former pilots, the precise technology he was describing remains unknown.

    The dispute comes amid growing pressure to modernize the FAA's aging infrastructure. On November 13, a telecommunications failure triggered a nationwide ground stop lasting nearly five hours. According to the FAA's subsequent investigation, excessive network traffic destabilized legacy equipment, affecting communications and radar feeds at 17 of the country's 22 enroute control centers. Approximately 12,500 flights were canceled that day, and hundreds more over the days that followed.

    In a recent development, on November 17, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, and Budget Director Russell Vought formally requested $50.1 billion from Congress. The proposal follows $12.5 billion approved in July 2025 and would finance technology upgrades, replacement facilities, and airport infrastructure. The administration's request is broken down as follows:.

    ATC technology and digital modernization.

    Airport infrastructure improvements.

    Five consolidated enroute control centers.

    Construction and upgrades of up to 140 ATC towers.

    The FAA aims to complete the first phase of its Brand New Air Traffic Control System by December 2028. However, in September, the Government Accountability Office warned that incomplete cost estimates and scheduling would undermine progress. Although the need for modernization is well documented, it does not establish that foreign controllers previously managed Trump's flights within US airspace. The president's renewed remarks therefore leave the original technical question unresolved.

    Breaking: FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.
    • Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

    The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

    In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, noted they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

    Sources indicate that “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”.

    According to recent reports, thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

    Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”.

    “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz stated. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”.

    Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing.

    The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

    “The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they remarked.

    They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

    Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

    In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

    “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter remarked.

    Industry observers note that on Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

    According to recent reports, “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related problems,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

    Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

    Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

    It has been revealed that “I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján stated, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”.

    Sources indicate that sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., remarked at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”.

    “I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that matter,” Moran said.

    Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

    #31171. Why The Flying Wing Never Became A Commercial Airliner

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1516 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why The Flying Wing Never Became A Commercial Airliner

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jack Northrop envisioned a sleek, tailless future when he sent the YB-49 aloft on October 21, 1947, stretching a 172-foot (52.4 meters) wing across the desert sky without a conventional fuselage or vertical stabilizer.
    • Despite the allure of an all-wing silhouette, commercial aviation stuck with cylindrical fuselages and tailed configurations that offered predictable handling, straightforward cabin pressurization, and familiar airport compatibility.
    • Converted from two piston-engined YB-35 airframes, the YB-49 stretched to a 172-foot (52.4-meter) wingspan and measured 53 feet, 1 inch (16.2 meters) in length, trading propeller drives for eight Allison J35 turbojets buried inside the wing, according to The Little Aviation Museum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jack Northrop envisioned a sleek, tailless future when he sent the YB-49 aloft on October 21, 1947, stretching a 172-foot (52.4 meters) wing across the desert sky without a conventional fuselage or vertical stabilizer. Promising lower drag and greater efficiency than traditional layouts, the experimental jet bomber nevertheless battled stability challenges before the second prototype crashed on June 5, 1948, killing all five crew members aboard and leading to the program winding down between 1949 and 1950.

    Despite the allure of an all-wing silhouette, commercial aviation stuck with cylindrical fuselages and tailed configurations that offered predictable handling, straightforward cabin pressurization, and familiar airport compatibility. Now that digital flight controls and blended-wing concepts are bringing tailless aerodynamics back into the spotlight, what technical, operational, and commercial hurdles still stand between a flying wing concept and a viable passenger airliner?

    Converted from two piston-engined YB-35 airframes, the YB-49 stretched to a 172-foot (52.4-meter) wingspan and measured 53 feet, 1 inch (16.2 meters) in length, trading propeller drives for eight Allison J35 turbojets buried inside the wing, according to The Little Aviation Museum. Removing a conventional fuselage and tail assembly allowed almost the entire planform to contribute to lift with reduced parasite drag, helping the prototype reach roughly 493 mph (793 km/h). At the same time, early turbojet fuel burn and internal volume tradeoffs tempered its range and payload flexibility relative to piston-powered designs.

    Recent findings suggest that flying without a tall vertical tail meant the YB-49 had less natural stability in yaw and had delicate pitch and roll-yaw coupling, including dutch roll, during turbulent air, maneuvers, and simulated bombing runs. As noted by MiGFlug, four small vertical fins were fitted to aid directional damping, though in the late 1940s crews relied on mechanical linkages and human coordination rather than high-speed digital flight control computers to manage continuous stability corrections.

    It has been revealed that after its maiden flight on October 21, 1947, the program flew only two converted airframes before the second prototype crashed on June 5, 1948, claiming the lives of all five crew members on board. Production orders were canceled in 1949 as Air Force leadership shifted toward competing bomber programs, and formal flight testing concluded in March 1950 before the surviving airframes were scrapped.

    According to recent reports, for an aerodynamically unstable tailless wing to become a dependable aircraft and actually work, it requires replacing purely mechanical linkages with high-speed digital fly-by-wire flight-control computers. Motion sensors can continuously measure aircraft attitude and rate changes, feeding real-time data to flight computers that command rapid, micro-adjusted deflections across trailing-edge control surfaces. That closed-loop automation damps pitch, yaw, and dutch roll oscillations far faster and more consistently than manual pilot inputs alone could achieve in earlier eras.

    Recent findings suggest that digital flight control design made the Northrop B-2 Spirit possible by allowing a pure flying wing to achieve low-observable radar signatures without needing a conventional vertical tail. Instead of using a large fin that would compromise stealth, the B-2 uses computer-coordinated elevons and split drag rudders to generate controlled yawing moments and maintain crisp handling across varying weights and flight regimes. Computing redundancy and sensor voting became foundational to keeping a naturally neutral or unstable wing profile predictable from takeoff through landing.

    Recent findings suggest that decades later, the Northrop B-21 Raider extends that digital control lineage into a modern low-observable bomber program built on newer avionics and computing architectures. The B-2 and B-21 demonstrate that computerized flight controls conquered the core stability and control challenges of tailless military aircraft, but solving stability in a combat airframe did not automatically translate into an airline cabin, and how to make it a reality.

    Sources indicate that the pure flying wing has not necessarily been revived, but JetZero is advancing the Z4 as a blended wing body (BWB) concept designed to carry roughly 230 to 250 passengers by smoothly merging a wide, lifting center body into outer wings. The program has gained traction through a $235 million US Air Force award supporting full-scale demonstrator development alongside intends to establish manufacturing operations in North Carolina. With a full-scale demonstrator targeted to fly in late 2027, the roadmap aims for commercial entry into service in the early 2030s if technical and regulatory hurdles are cleared on schedule.

    Industry observers note that commercial interest in the Z4 is very real, and carriers such as Japan Airlines and United Airlines have made agreements to support the development of the aircraft. For airlines evaluating next-generation single-aisle and midsize replacements, a BWB promises lower drag and reduced fuel burn per seat compared with conventional tube-and-wing layouts. Making those conditional fleet commitments become firm deliveries, however, depends on proving that the airframe can meet strict safety, manufacturing, and operational standards at scale.

    Propulsion integration sits near the center of that verification effort, including a November 2026 report from Leeham News noting that the FAA is funding a study into top-mounted engine airflow for JetZero's design. Placing engines above the aft airframe can help shield noise, but maintaining clean airflow and stable engine operation across flight conditions remains a critical engineering focus ahead of commercial certification.

    A cylindrical tube naturally resists internal cabin pressure by distributing hoop stress evenly around a circular cross-section, whereas a wide, flattened wing-body hull faces far higher bending and pressure-loading demands. A non-cylindrical cabin shell tends to bow outward when pressurized at cruise altitude, so to compensate, designers need to add structural reinforcement, internal bulkheads, or load-bearing frames that add mass and complexity.

    Emergency evacuation rules further add to cabin design complexity, particularly the regulatory requirement to evacuate a full aircraft within 90 seconds using half of the available exits, covered in Simple Flying analysis. Unlike a narrow single- or twin-aisle tube where passengers move linearly toward well-marked doors, a wide blended-wing cabin needs carefully engineered pathways, clear signage, and balanced exit placement, so travelers seated deep inside the layout can reach exits without bottlenecks. Cabin tiering across premium and economy zones also needs to align with aisle geometry and exit capacity rather than treating interior floor space as an open hall.

    In a recent development, on the ground, widebody wingspans around 213 feet (65 meters) must fit within existing terminal gate envelopes, taxiway clearances, and apron stand markings without forcing costly airport rebuilds. Even when a wide airframe clears wingspan limits at a standard widebody gate, its broader center section and altered fuselage contour can complicate jetbridge docking reach, de-icing access, and ground support vehicle positioning. Smooth ramp operations really depend on proving that turnaround tasks load and unload cleanly alongside conventional airliners.

    Recent findings suggest that within a wide, open cabin, the sensory rhythm of a flight changes compared with walking down a narrow, low-ceilinged aisle. Designers can shape the atmosphere through layered ambient lighting, tactile fabrics, and warmer material palettes that soften the industrial feel of long-haul travel and create distinct zones for rest, work, or socializing. When the interior feels less like a corridor and more like a curated living space, passenger stress often eases.

    Sightlines and motion perception play a major role in whether that spaciousness feels inviting or disorienting. Travelers seated further outboard from the centerline can notice more pronounced vertical movement when the aircraft banks or hits chop, making smooth cabin damping and calm visual anchors especially valuable. At the same time, passengers placed in central rows away from outer walls miss natural views of the horizon, requiring thoughtful lighting cues or digital view panels to keep the cabin feeling open and grounded.

    For airlines, an unconventional cabin layout offers a rare canvas for brand differentiation in a crowded market. Carriers can build an identity around quiet acoustics, signature color schemes, and tailored service rituals that signal innovation without feeling gimmicky. If passengers connect emotionally with the warmth and poise of the space, the cabin itself becomes part of the airline's promise, not something that needs to be explained to customers.

    It has been revealed that pure flying wings remained absent from passenger service because winning aerodynamic efficiency on paper is only half the battle when weighed against structural pressure loads, emergency evacuation rules, airport compatibility, and airline economics. Digital flight controls solved the stability hurdles that haunted the YB-49 and paved the way for stealth bombers, but turning a wide, wing-shaped cabin into a profitable, certified airliner is no easy task.

    Recent findings suggest that any manufacturer brave enough to try and make something like this has to solve practical constraints that circular fuselages and conventional tails handle with far less friction. Whether a blended wing body can actually fill that divide comes down to proving real-world reliability, passenger acceptance, and unit economics without turning every airport gate or cabin layout into a costly exception.

    The next major checkpoints arrive with full-scale demonstrator flight testing targeted for late 2027 and potential commercial entry into service in the early 2030s. If JetZero or other ventures like Nautilus can validate aerodynamic performance, propulsion integration, and regulatory certification along that timeline, blended-wing designs could finally move from aviation curiosity to active airline fleets.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific. The two carriers announced a new interline partnership that will allow travelers to combine flights on both airlines under a single ticket.

    Sources indicate that the agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S. The partnership will provide connections through French Bee’s three U.S. gateway airports that Southwest also serves: Los Angeles, Miami, and San Francisco.

    French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.

    Passengers will be able to connect between French Bee’s international flights and Southwest domestic flights without having to purchase separate tickets for each airline or recheck bags at each airline.

    French Bee operates an all-Airbus A350 fleet, with its primary hub located at Paris-Orly Airport, and operations to North America and destinations in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

    Southwest passengers will gain access to French Bee destinations not only from Paris, but also Tahiti in French Polynesia, which the French carrier flies to from San Francisco. The partnership will also offer one-stop French Bee connections from Paris to the Maldives and Sri Lanka, scheduled to launch in December 2026, along with current flights to Reunion Island.

    In a recent development, for French Bee customers, the fresh arrangement provides access to a much larger network of domestic destinations throughout the U.S. Southwest’s network includes cities such as Las Vegas, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Nashville, Austin, San Diego, Phoenix, and multiple destinations in the Hawaiian Islands.

    The agreement represents another step in Southwest’s expanding international connectivity strategy, as the airline continues to develop relationships with overseas carriers rather than rely exclusively on its own international operations with its all-Boeing 737 fleet.

    Tickets for connecting flights are now available through French Bee’s website.

    • Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov.
    • Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen.
    • Industry observers note that democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders mentioned Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care strategy if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

    Industry observers note that democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

    Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

    His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

    The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

    According to recent reports, “If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders remarked, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

    Sources indicate that sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

    According to recent reports, while who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders stated he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

    Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”.

    Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

    It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

    To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

    Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”.

    Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee problems, he looks forward to finding common ground.

    #31164. Industry News: Aviation Gems: The Airbus A380 Is The Largest, But The Boeing 747-8 Actually Holds 2 Worldwide Titles

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1504 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Aviation Gems: The Airbus A380 Is The Largest, But The Boeing 747-8 Actually Holds 2 Worldwide Titles

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the introduction of the Airbus A380 historically dethroned Boeing as the reigning champion of big jet builders.
    • Boeing responded not with a brand-upcoming double-decker, but by stretching its classic 747 design into the 747-8 Intercontinental.
    • Industry observers note that however, while the Boeing jet carried fewer passengers and weighed hundreds of thousands of pounds less, it quietly held onto two major world records that the massive A380 could never take away.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the introduction of the Airbus A380 historically dethroned Boeing as the reigning champion of big jet builders. However, that statement comes with a couple of caveats. It is true that the A380 beats the classic Boeing 747 in wingspan, height, weight, and passenger capacity, but the long-reigning 'queen of the skies' was not made irrelevant overnight.

    Boeing responded not with a brand-upcoming double-decker, but by stretching its classic 747 design into the 747-8 Intercontinental. With two full passenger decks running from nose to tail, the European superjumbo dwarfed every competitor in wingspan, tail height, weight, and seating capacity. On paper, it looked as though Airbus had swept every major size and performance record in commercial flying.

    Industry observers note that however, while the Boeing jet carried fewer passengers and weighed hundreds of thousands of pounds less, it quietly held onto two major world records that the massive A380 could never take away. First, by extending the fuselage, Boeing made the 747-8 the longest airliner in service, measuring 250 feet 2 inches (76.25 meters) from nose to tail.

    This made it over 11 feet longer than the A380. Second, thanks to its sharply swept wings and modern engines, the 747-8 cruises at Mach 0.855 (about 567 mph), edging out the A380’s Mach 0.85 pace to claim the title of the fastest commercial jetliner flying today.

    Recent findings suggest that for one pragmatic reason, airport gates, Boeing decided to make the 747-8 longer rather than wider. Because the A380 has such an enormous wingspan, major airports had to widen taxiways and build special two-story boarding bridges just to handle it. Boeing kept the 747-8’s wingspan narrower at 224 feet 5 inches, allowing it to pull into standard international gates with minimal airport upgrades.

    Industry observers note that boeing extended the earlier 747-400 body by 18.3 feet (5.6 meters) to create the 747-8, the longest aircraft in the sky. Two extra fuselage sections were added by engineers, one in front of and one behind the wings, increasing the overall length to 250 feet 2 inches (76.25 meters).

    The 747-8 surpassed the Airbus A380 by about 11.5 feet (3.5 meters) in terms of its additional length, surpassing the previous record set by the 75.36-meter Airbus A340-600. While a four-engine Boeing remained expensive to fly, the 747-8's gate compatibility still gave airlines a practical edge over the A380.

    Because the superjumbo required costly terminal upgrades and triggered higher size-based airport fees, its route map was limited to a small group of mega-hubs. By staying within standard widebody gate limits and weighing far less, the 747-8 carried over 400 passengers into a wider range of international airports with slightly lower ground costs.

    Recent findings suggest that boeing’s second trump card over the Airbus colossus comes down to its cruising speed world title. Rated at Mach 0.855, or roughly 567 mph at 35,000 feet, the 747-8 is the fastest commercial airliner flying today, edging out the Airbus A380, A350, and Boeing 787 at Mach 0.85, as well as the 777 at Mach 0.84.

    While a speed advantage of under 1% only trims a few minutes off a long flight, it gives pilots helpful schedule padding against headwinds and arrival delays. That speed advantage comes straight from a 1960s design decision. When Boeing engineers first shaped the 747, they expected supersonic jets like Concorde to take over passenger travel.

    As such, they angled the 747's wings sharply backward to help it cruise faster and keep up with high-speed air traffic. Four General Electric GEnx engines provide the power needed to take full advantage of that high-speed wing. Adapted from the Boeing 787 Dreamliner program, these modern engines produce strong thrust while burning less fuel than older 747 powerplants.

    While straight wings work best at lower speeds, swept-back wings slice through high-altitude air with far less wind resistance, a shape Boeing kept on the 747-8 alongside modern, fuel-saving raked wingtips. Paired with the wing, the powerplants allow the 747-8 to cruise comfortably at Mach 0.855 without hitting the drag penalties that slow down wider, less aggressively swept airliners.

    Stretching a classic fuselage to over 250 feet in length created unexpected engineering headaches during early test flights. When pilots pushed the prototype 747-8 to high speeds, the longer body and redesigned wings experienced troublesome vibrations along the wingtips. Fixing that flexing forced Boeing to reinforce internal structures and rewrite flight-control software.

    This pushed deliveries more than two years behind schedule and added over $2 billion in program costs. Once flight-test results were in, fuel economy turned out to be an even greater problem. The promised fuel-burn targets were not met by the new GEnx engines by 2.7%. That seemingly small miss wiped out the narrow cost advantage Boeing needed to convince airlines to buy a 747 instead of twinjets like the 777.

    In a recent development, the tension exploded in September 2011, when launch customer Cargolux abruptly walked out of delivery ceremonies and refused to accept its first two jets until Boeing and General Electric offered financial discounts. Watching from the sidelines, passenger airlines grew wary of four-engine fuel and maintenance bills, choosing twinjets or the A380 instead and leaving the passenger 747-8 with very few orders.

    In a recent development, the two biggest passenger flagships in the world have different design philosophies, which can be seen by comparing them side by side. Airbus's A380 can accommodate about 525 seats in conventional layouts thanks to its enormous maximum takeoff weight of 1,268,000 lb (575,155 kg) and two full passenger decks.

    The Boeing 747-8, on the other hand, trades raw capacity for cheaper airport fees and easier ground logistics throughout a 410-seat cabin by capping its takeoff weight at 987,000 lb (447,700 kg). Depending on how their wings fit actual airport gates, airlines use the two aircraft in different ways.

    Lufthansa, the only carrier flying both types in significant numbers, keeps all 17 of its 747-8s in Frankfurt for routes to cities like Newark, Tokyo, and Johannesburg, where the jet slips into standard gates without special infrastructure. Meanwhile, Lufthansa flies its eight A380s out of Munich to massive hubs like Los Angeles and Delhi, where airports have widened taxiways and dual-level jet bridges built for the superjumbo's wider wingspan.

    The 747-8’s slight speed edge also shapes daily flight planning across winter jet streams. Cruising at Mach 0.855 allows dispatchers to trim a few valuable minutes off twelve-hour westbound flights compared to the A380, helping protect passenger connections when departures face ground delays. However, even that operational flexibility could not shield the four-engine jet from brutal economic headwinds whenever cabins flew with empty seats.

    Recent findings suggest that in order to build the longest airliner in history, a challenging engineering conundrum had to be resolved: how to extend length without increasing debilitating weight? In response, Boeing developed aluminum-lithium skin panels that stiffened the stretched fuselage against repeated cabin pressurization while reducing metal density by 10%.

    In a recent development, across the Atlantic, Airbus used GLARE, a composite laminate of glass and aluminum fibers that stops minuscule cracks throughout its massive double-deck hull, to address weight and durability on the A380. Equally different priorities are reflected in their wing designs.

    8,200 nautical miles (15,186 km).

    7,370 nautical miles (13,650 km).

    It has been revealed that in order to reduce drag during long-haul cruise, Boeing replaced the upright winglets of the 747-400 with sweeping composite raked wingtips. By contrast, Airbus fitted the A380 with small vertical wingtip fences, leaning on an enormous 9,100-square-foot wing area to lift up to 575 tons into the sky.

    To protect those long wings in flight, Boeing paired traditional mechanical cables with latest computer-controlled actuators on the outer wing surfaces. During turbulence, the system automatically deploys wing spoilers to absorb bending forces, and at high cruising speeds it locks outer control surfaces in place to stop the wing vibrations seen in early testing.

    For both aircraft manufacturers, producing the largest aircraft in commercial history came at an incredible financial cost. Before completing more than 50 years of 747 manufacturing in January 2023 and delivering its last cargo to Atlas Air after producing 155 of the stretched aircraft, Boeing had to endure nearly $4.2 billion in accounting losses on the 747-8.

    According to recent reports, as airlines switched from four-engine behemoths to fuel-efficient twinjets, Airbus suffered an even worse blow after investing more than $30 billion in the A380 and closing its manufacturing line in December 2021 after just 251 deliveries. With both assembly lines closed, the 747-8 stands alone as the fastest and longest commercial airliner flying today, marking the final peak of four-engine design.

    In a recent development, still, its length record has an expiration date. Stretching 251 feet 9 inches (76.7 meters), about 19 inches longer than the 747-8, Boeing’s upcoming twin-engine 777-9 packs massive GE9X engines and folding wingtips to carry over 400 passengers at a fraction of the fuel cost.

    Breaking: Restored to Calder’s blueprint, the clouds are spinning again

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday.
    • The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.
    • Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

    Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

    It has been revealed that “It’s totally phenomenal,” he mentioned, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”.

    It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

    According to recent reports, rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

    According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”.

    It has been revealed that “It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”.

    In a recent development, it was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

    Sources indicate that “We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he mentioned. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”.

    Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

    Recent findings suggest that “We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how major this was until it demonstrated up on their doorstep.”.

    Quilici noted he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

    “Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

    Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

    Sources indicate that “This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement stated.

    The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

    “It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” mentioned Kim Shirley.

    In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

    Industry observers note that but when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and noted he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

    Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

    “Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower mentioned.

    It has been revealed that according to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The latest clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

    “These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he noted.

    Recent findings suggest that younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

    “I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

    Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

    “I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he mentioned, gazing up at it.

    Lufthansa Group plans to lay off around 1,000 full-time workers at its flagship carrier as elevated fuel prices and service disruptions continue to undercut earnings.

    Industry observers note that the airline group disclosed the cuts in a letter sent to employees and seen by Dow Jones Newswire, according to The Wall Street Journal. The reductions will target Lufthansa’s hubs in Frankfurt and Munich.

    Company leaders remarked their 2024 turnaround initiative, initially expected to boost earnings by €2.5 billion over four years, is no longer enough to keep the brand on solid financial ground.

    “The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action, and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation,” the letter said.

    Recent findings suggest that lufthansa failed to reach an agreement with its pilot union earlier this week, setting the stage for a possible work stoppage. The impasse has already resulted in two short strikes, one in February, the other in March.

    Lufthansa Group has spoken openly about the damage caused by higher fuel prices over the last nine months. Over the summer, it retired aircraft, cut routes, and warned that layoffs were likely unless prices eased.

    According to EuroNews, Lufthansa has lost on average about €20 million per month since the start of the year.
