    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.
    • The carrier remarked Friday that it will restart flights from Latest York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027.
    • American has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.

    The carrier remarked Friday that it will restart flights from Latest York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027. Flights will operate daily using Boeing 777-200ER aircraft.

    American has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023. It remained on the sidelines even as rivals United and Delta resumed service to Ben Gurion International Airport, though they too were forced to temporarily pause flights during fighting between Israel and Iran.

    Israeli officials had questioned why American was slow to reconnect the country, citing the importance of air links between Tel Aviv and Fresh York. The airline did not offer an explanation beyond concern for the safety of its passengers and crew.

    American also noted Friday that it has formed a commercial partnership with Tel Aviv-based low-cost carrier Israir. The agreement will expand in phases over time, American said; in the first phase, Israir will place its code on American’s flights between JFK and Tel Aviv.

    The carriers will also work to implement an interline agreement that would give Israir customers access to American’s network across the U.S., Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean from JFK.

    “American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire,” American Senior Vice President of Alliances Anmol Bhargava said in a news release. “As we prepare to resume service between Fresh York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”.

    Sources indicate that israir operates five weekly flights between JFK and Tel Aviv using Airbus A330-200 aircraft. New York is its only U.S. destination; most of its network is concentrated in the Near East and Europe.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, ‘E verything’s Up to Date in Kansas City” — that few minutes of pure effervescence in Oklahoma refers to Kansas City circa 1907, when it was in the middle of its version of the City Beautiful movement.
    • I visited last month and saw the very enjoyable exhibition American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today.
    • Allen is National Review’s art critic.

    According to recent reports, ‘E verything’s Up to Date in Kansas City” — that few minutes of pure effervescence in Oklahoma refers to Kansas City circa 1907, when it was in the middle of its version of the City Beautiful movement. New boulevards, new, fancy neighborhoods, hundreds of fountains, and much more were in the works. The sparkle of a new art museum was in the civic eye, too. The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art didn’t open its doors until 1933, but better late than never. It’s an essential visit for art lovers.

    I visited last month and saw the very enjoyable exhibition American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today. It presents Joel Sternfeld’s lovely, often sad, wry, late-1970s and early-1980s landscape photographs in the context of the American landscape-photography genre. I love Sternfeld’s work. Born in 1944, he was the cutting-edge photographer who took color landscape photography mainstream, mostly through American Prospects, his portfolio of photographs published in book form in 1987. Color? Cutting-edge in the ’80s? Well, 1987 is about to be 40 years ago, so it qualifies as days of yore, and what has became American Prospects started in the late ’70s, when Sternfeld started an epic road trip to make art about Americans and the land. Landscape photography was, à la Ansel Adams, commonly in black and white, thought to evoke grandeur and mystery. What pushed Sternfeld to color was the advent of Kodak Vericolor III film in the 1970s. It delivered accurate, vibrant color and was good for various lighting and especially skin tones.

    It has been revealed that brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

    On “Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum”.

    #31158. Breaking: Here's How Much The 787 Dreamliner Heavily Influenced Boeing's 747-8 Development

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1618 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Here's How Much The 787 Dreamliner Heavily Influenced Boeing's 747-8 Development

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that when Boeing launched the 747-8 in November 2005, it presented the airplane as a stretched, re-winged, and re-engined update of the 747-400 that would use technology borrowed from the 787 Dreamliner.
    • It has been revealed that rather than commissioning an all-upcoming quadjet for a limited market, Boeing chose to graft selected Dreamliner innovations onto a familiar airframe, which kept development costs manageable and preserved the operating familiarity that long-time 747 customers valued.
    • According to recent reports, the most substantial transfer from the 787 program came through the powerplants.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that when Boeing launched the 747-8 in November 2005, it presented the airplane as a stretched, re-winged, and re-engined update of the 747-400 that would use technology borrowed from the 787 Dreamliner. The Dreamliner program had been launched only a year earlier, and its work on lightweight composites, efficient engines, and electronically managed systems gave Boeing a supply of proven solutions at the moment the aging jumbo needed them.

    It has been revealed that rather than commissioning an all-upcoming quadjet for a limited market, Boeing chose to graft selected Dreamliner innovations onto a familiar airframe, which kept development costs manageable and preserved the operating familiarity that long-time 747 customers valued. The resulting aircraft differs from its predecessor in several visible ways, yet it remains a 747 in its structure and in the way it is flown, so a fair assessment of the Dreamliner’s influence requires examining each major system in turn. That review shows a program that borrowed boldly where performance was at stake and conservatively wherever certification, cost, or pilot familiarity argued for restraint.

    Wikimedia Commons, Simple Flying.

    According to recent reports, the most substantial transfer from the 787 program came through the powerplants. The 747-8 uses four General Electric GEnx-2B67 engines, a smaller-diameter relative of the GEnx developed for the Dreamliner. The design emphasizes a high bypass ratio, sending most of the air around the core to generate thrust more efficiently than the lower-bypass engines of earlier generations.

    Sources indicate that engineers modified the design so that each engine could supply bleed air, the compressed air tapped from the engine to run onboard systems, because the 747 still depends on a conventional pneumatic architecture that the 787 largely abandoned in favor of electrical power. Each engine generates 66,500 pounds (30,164 kg) of thrust and carries a 105-inch (267 cm) composite fan, a material choice that cuts weight relative to metallic blades.

    GEnx-1B vs. GEnx-2B Technical Comparison.

    Sawtooth-shaped edges called chevrons line the rear of the engine housing, borrowing a noise-reduction device from the 787 that encourages exhaust and bypass air to blend more gradually. Noise also carries financial weight, since many airports levy charges tied to certified noise levels, and Boeing has said the 747-8 produces a considerably smaller noise footprint than the 747-400.

    Sharing a design lineage with the 787 engine allowed Boeing and GE to spread development effort across two programs rather than funding a bespoke powerplant for a model expected to sell in modest numbers. Unlike the Dreamliner, which Boeing offers with a choice between GE and Rolls-Royce engines, the 747-8 is offered only with the GEnx-2B, which spared Boeing the cost of certifying a second powerplant for a modest order book. For operators, the engine change translated into lower fuel burn and emissions per seat than the 747-400, which formed the core of the airplane’s commercial pitch to airlines and cargo carriers.

    Boeing designed a latest wing for the 747-8 with fresh airfoil shapes intended to improve aerodynamic efficiency at cruise. Designing a wing for a derivative airplane also imposes constraints that a clean-sheet program avoids, because the new surface had to mate with the existing fuselage architecture, which limited how far the planform could depart from the 747-400’s.

    According to recent reports, at the tips, the upright winglets of the 747-400 gave way to raked wingtips, the same approach used on the 777 and the 787. Sweeping the tip aft reduces drag generated by wingtip vortices while adding less weight than a taller vertical surface would. The configuration debuted on the 767-400ER, which means the 747-8 inherited it from a lineage broader than the Dreamliner alone.

    Boeing attributes the 747-8’s higher cruising speed relative to the 747-400 to the combined effect of the wing, wingtips, and engines. The gain matters to passenger carriers flying long routes, where minutes accumulate into meaningful time savings. The aerodynamic gains in cruise efficiency also translate directly into range or payload, which matters especially for the freighter, where operators trade fuel against cargo on long sectors.

    The larger wing extends the span to roughly 224 feet (68.27 meters), compared with about 211 feet (64.31 meters) on the 747-400, a growth that supports the airplane’s higher maximum takeoff weight. Aerodynamic refinement of this kind typically yields incremental gains, yet on an airplane that burns many tons of fuel on every long flight, even small improvements compound into sizable savings over a fleet’s life.

    Wikimedia Commons, Simple Flying.

    The 747-8 also adopted elements of the 787’s fly-by-wire philosophy, in which pilot inputs travel as electrical signals to flight control computers rather than moving surfaces through mechanical cables and pulleys. Electronic signaling reduces weight, since cable runs and associated hardware can be shortened, and it allows computers to modulate surface movements for smoother handling and greater structural efficiency.

    The shift follows a broader pattern within the firm, since the 777 was Boeing’s first fly-by-wire airliner and the 787 extended that approach more thoroughly. Boeing applied the technology selectively because it wanted qualified pilots on the 747-400 to move to the fresh model easily. The flight deck therefore keeps a layout and control feel close to its predecessor’s.

    Training pilots on an unfamiliar type requires simulator time, instructor capacity, and revenue flying hours that airlines would rather devote to scheduled service, so commonality functions as a quiet but substantial financial benefit for operators already flying the 747-400, whose crews can serve both types. The Dreamliner, by contrast, was free to adopt an entirely upcoming flight deck, a freedom the 747-8 deliberately did not exercise.

    The passenger version of the 747-8 received an interior inspired by the Dreamliner’s. Curved, upswept ceiling panels give the cabin a more spacious feel, and LED lighting that runs the length of the cabin can shift color to suggest different times of day. Airlines adopt such lighting and ceiling cues largely because they believe the surroundings can ease fatigue on long sectors, though the benefit is difficult to measure objectively. Windows are larger than those on the 747-400, which improves natural light and passenger views, although they remain smaller than the Dreamliner’s distinctive dimmable windows.

    Recent findings suggest that the most visible change for many travelers is the staircase to the upper deck. The classic 747’s narrow spiral staircase has been replaced by a wide, curved staircase that is easier to use and gives the entry area a more open, premium character. The interior upgrades arrived alongside an 18-foot-4-inch (5.5 meters) fuselage stretch, which lets Boeing quote a typical three-class capacity of 467 passengers. The stretch also lengthened the upper deck, giving airlines additional space for premium seating.

    Despite the heavy borrowing, the 747-8 does not share the Dreamliner’s defining structural feature. The 787 builds its fuselage from carbon fiber composites, whereas the 747-8 remains an aluminum airframe, consistent with the metallic construction of every earlier 747. The decision carries consequences that passengers can feel. Because composite structures resist corrosion and fatigue better than aluminum, the Dreamliner can maintain a lower cabin altitude and higher humidity than conventional metal airplanes, benefits the 747-8 does not offer.

    Retaining aluminum made commercial sense. A composite fuselage would have required a new manufacturing process, new tooling, and a fresh certification effort for a program that was never expected to reach the volumes of a mainstream twin-aisle jet. Boeing instead reused the structure and production methods established over decades at its Everett factory, where the 747 had been built since the late 1960s.

    Sources indicate that boeing also preserved many systems in common with the 747-400, a choice that simplifies maintenance, spares provisioning, and mechanic training for airlines operating both models. The freighter, which accounts for the majority of 747-8 deliveries, retains the hinged nose door that lets long loads enter straight along the main deck.

    In a recent development, the 747-8 shows that technology transfer, when applied with discipline and clear commercial goals, can extend an airframe’s commercial life without the expense of starting over. The final aircraft left the production line in early 2023 after 155 had been built. Its more durable influence may appear in cargo operations, where the freighters seem likely to remain in service for decades. Few alternatives offer comparable volume, and the Dreamliner-derived engines should keep operating costs competitive as fleets age in the years ahead.

    Sustainable aviation fuel offers a further lever for extending service lives, because engines of the GEnx generation are approved for blends with conventional jet fuel, which lets operators reduce lifecycle emissions without modifying the airplane. Market pressure shapes what comes next, since fuel efficiency and emissions goals increasingly favor twin-engine aircraft, so the quadjet is unlikely to return as a clean-sheet design, and the 747-8’s lasting contribution may be as the final demonstration of how far a four-engine airliner could be pushed with the technology of its time.

    It has been revealed that the 747-8 program also previews how Boeing is likely to modernize mature designs in the future. The 777X, for example, pairs a newly introduced composite wing with new engines on a fuselage descended from the 777, a pattern that mirrors the 747-8’s selective borrowing but moves much further toward composite structure. For engineers, the more transferable lesson concerns what to share and what to withhold.

    Components that improve efficiency without altering certification basis or pilot procedures, such as engines, aerodynamic surfaces, and lighting, moved across freely, while anything that would have disrupted commonality with the 747-400 stayed behind. Future derivatives are likely to follow the same filter, with the cost of recertification acting as the main gatekeeper, and the 747-8 supplies the clearest template of that logic.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

    Seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom unveiled Friday.

    Industry observers note that seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

    “He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

    It has been revealed that jonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

    Gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

    In a recent development, american will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A newly introduced reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be unveiled in December.

    “For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

    The changes follow a broader management reshuffle confirmed in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

    Tech Report: Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May.
    • Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the glitch is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.
    • “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the glitch is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

    “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

    Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

    Recent findings suggest that at glitch is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Upcoming York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

    Sources indicate that advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly remarked it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

    Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they proposal to bring up a vote next year.

    Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

    Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

    The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

    “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

    “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

    Sources indicate that trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

    While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

    Sources indicate that “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most key stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

    The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the glitch.

    “Across the political spectrum,” the letter mentioned, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series.
    • Recent findings suggest that have an idea for a livery that we should highlight?
    • Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

    Recent findings suggest that have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

    Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

    The airline unveiled its new corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

    The most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

    Recent findings suggest that the fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

    Iberia’s new branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

    According to recent reports, the redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

    Recent findings suggest that the first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The newly introduced appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

    Industry observers note that iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

    The current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

    In a recent development, iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A upcoming deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.
    • Industry observers note that the county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations.
    • According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A upcoming deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

    Industry observers note that the county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

    According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The newly introduced lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper said.

    The airline plans to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

    “Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

    American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.
